title: TheChirurgeon's Road Through 2026, Part 41: Testing Death Guard Point Drops
content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I talked about painting models using the new Tone Pro Paints - they're pretty good - but if you want a deeper dive or more involved review of them, you can find our full first impressions review here.

The big news this week is the release of the September 2026 Balance update, which gives us a ton of Detachment and Point changes but also updates Chaos Marines and Grey Knights to match the statline changes for space marines. We wrote a full review of it this week, and in it I talked about how much I liked the changes to Death Guard. Today I'm going to explore that, and the impact on the game I played.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Friendship Ended with Thousand Sons

This week's updates were a mixed bag for the chaos factions but were particularly rough on the Thousand Sons - Scarabs and Rubrics took serious point hikes, along with the characters you'd attach to those units. This is a nasty set of point hikes to my army specifically, which also was, notably, not very good - I wasn't impressed with how Rubricae Phalanx played (though I definitely wasn't playing the best version of it), and it took a brutal hit. There are probably Thousand Sons lists that can get there waiting to be built, but they likely rely much more on Tzaangor Enlightened and Tzaangors - units I just don't have painted at the moment.

Pair that with the oncoming rush of sudden feel no pains against Psychic attacks and it felt like a good time to rotate back off Thousand Sons. I've had a good run with them at Tacoma, the Lone Star Open, and Challengers Cup, but I think it's time to look at other armies in my stable.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Death Guard Are My New Best Friend

On the other hand, the new point drops on Death Guard were intriguing! Death Guard are an army that have struggled in 11th edition so far: They lost -1 to hit as a contagion ability and only recently regained a worse version of it, they've had restrictive detachment rules, and they've just been a little too expensive, with their durability not amounting to much. That said, the only real buffs they got in the new update were to bolter and melee weapon strength, and as a result, most of their point costs dropped. I started tooling around with lists, looking to understand how to take advantage of cheaper terminators and terminator characters as well as PBCs - the Plagueburst Crawler is still a very underrated unit in the Death Guard arsenal, in my estimation.

After some tooling, here's what I came up with for a test game:

The general idea here is that all the Drones and Haulers have [ASSAULT] from their Detachment rule. The Defiler can strip cover and is a priority target, the PBCs grind forward and shoot, the Deathshroud teleport in and use the Hammer Detachment rule to open up gaps that the Poxwalkers can't, and the army can just be faster and deadlier than it looks. There are a lot of vehicles here, and it's a bit of a stat check in that regard. That said, these vehicles have a lot of hitting power as well, and can do surprising damage in melee in a pinch.

Exported with App Version: v2.7.0 (1), Data Version: v963

T's Thoughts: It's good for PA and terrible for Recon. Probably needs Novis to protect scout move since otherwise the deployment zone is too crowded for 7 tanks.

I'm Going First

That's good here - Purge generally wants that, so the reserves drop in sooner. It's better into Priority Assets than Recon, but T chose to test Recon in this mission. The good news is I'm familiar with the mission after Challengers Cup - you need to consecrate three objectives early and hold off your opponent from Triangulating before round 4.

I push up early with the goal of saturating the board with threats and locking down T's action units - he doesn't have a lot of sisters, just a lot of tanks, and if I kill the sisters that will leave him unable to Triangulate effectively with chaff units. I lose the Defiler on turn 1 but that ends up being OK - it takes two units and Vahl to bring it down (I did not pass many saves with it), and that pulls fire off the PBCs and Blight-Haulers. I use my Poxwalkers to harass T's units and get a turn 1 charge off on one of his Immolators to mess up T's movement plans.

Despite my excellent turn 2, Sisters remain an army which can do insane amounts of damage off a very small number of units. T picks up about half my army with the remianing third of his, and suddenly the game looks much more like a stalemate than it did a few moments prior.

The play of the game happens when I get the 7" charge off my Deathshrouds into Vahl's unit, picking them up with melee damage. I'd been slowly closing in around the rest of the table with the rest of my army, pushing T back into the lower right corner. Vahl's unit going down was a backbreaker, and while T still had the Castigator and an Exorcist to do damage, the net result is that it's too late. Early splash damage form the mortars helped turn decent damage from the MBHs and Bloat-Drones into Lethal Damage when those hit.

What won me this game is pure, stupid volume. That second and third wave of Terminators made a huge difference, dropping in when I needed them and taking out ke targets while forcing T to hang back and screen out his deployment zone to prevent a 6" deep strike. Meanwhile having [ASSAULT] on all the vehicles was huge - I had a ton of movement on early turns to run around the table, and being able to move through walls on top of that enabled some crazy options.

Result: Win, 98-45

Tweaking the List

After the game I took a look at the list and worked through what I wanted to change. I had room to work with for enhancements, but the only ones I'd consider are Shriekworm Familiar and Tendrilous Emissions - and I'm already attaching the Lord of Virulence.

What it boiled down to was the question: Is the Defiler better than two units that aggregate to more/similar output? Dropping the Defiler plus the 40 points I had left over was enough to buy a third Plagueburst Crawler (one with double plague spitters), and a third unit of 3 Deathshroud, or upgrade to 6. I really like adding the PBC and a unit of 3 Deathshroud at the moment - the sheer volume of units that gives me with 2+ saves and high toughness is legit, creating a nasty stat check on the opponent while still being very mobile.

So that's my next iteration - the same two characters, each attached to a unit of Deathshroud, but I'm running 3 each of Deathshroud x3 / PBCs / MBHs / HBLs and two units of Poxwalkers. It's more or less the list I ran last year when I won my first GT with Death Guard, give or take a few tweaks, and I really like the sheer volume of units it can bring with the increased mobility. Except it has one more entire unit of Deathshroud, which is a hell of an add. I think that's just a shitload of value to be able to bring to the table, having 14 unit drops, all of which have to be dealt with - and the ones that don't move 10" either have Infiltrators or Deep Strike. It's good stuff.

I'm going to test again next week but if I'm not seeing the results I want I'll likely look instead at swapping out the third PBC for something more efficient - the next choice is a third unit of Poxwalkers and a Predator, where I'd get similar firepower output at a lower cost while adding a third objective holder unit. That said, I really like the idea of a third PBC with spitters to rumble up the middle of the table and pile on a third activation of indirect mortar splash.

Final Thoughts

That's it for this week. This weekend I'm heading off to the 2026 Las Vegas Open but I'm not actually planning to play Warhammer this weekend; I'm there for a variety of business development tasks, saying hi to people and schmoozing on behalf of Tabletop Battles. And also kind of just on a weekend vacation with the missus, so while I considered playing in the GT, I decided against it - at best I'd play Friday and drop after three rounds, which seemed like a waste. Next year, maybe.

See you Thursday.

title: Marvel Crisis Protocol Through the Years: The Biggest Rules Changes, Revisited
content:
Marvel Crisis Protocol hasn’t officially had a second edition, but for those who have been playing since the early days, it certainly feels as though enough has changed to call the current game “2.0.” No, we’ve never seen huge, monumental shifts drop in one go (though we’ve come close a few times), but Atomic Mass Games has delivered fairly consistent, impactful updates that, combined, have become more than the sum of their parts.

Even more impressive, these changes have been almost universally praised as positive moves for the games. For those who have been around a while, revisiting the way things used to be might feel a bit nostalgic. Newer players might be surprised by how different parts of MCP used to be. Regardless, join me as we walk through a vaguely chronological retelling of how things used to be, discuss their overall impact on the game, and talk about why the change worked (or didn’t) to make MCP a better overall experience. Note: This doesn’t include every change that’s happened, but it covers the major ones.

Early Tweaks to Roster Construction

The first rules change for MCP was small but had meaningful implications. Originally, players would include ten characters (and six Crises) but only eight Team Tactics Cards. This added consistency was simply easier to remember, but it also allowed for slightly more variety as more cards were released for the game. In hindsight, the change totally makes sense. Will Shick has mentioned that, originally, the development team didn’t expect Team Tactics Cards to be such a competitively impactful part of the game. That quickly proved wrong, and ten remains a good-feeling sweet spot for including commonly played staples and situational tech cards.

The Banned and Restricted List

The MCP banned and restricted list has sort of ebbed and flowed in importance over the years, but at the beginning, it didn’t exist at all. As one might expect, this led to a handful of generic (not locked to a specific Affiliation or character) cards dominating competitive play and pushing many other options out. To open up roster diversity and let Affiliations showcase more of their unique cards, AMG introduced Restricted cards in late 2020. Along with it, they also outright banned one TTC that was proving too powerful and prolific.

The very first B&R List was as follows:

Restricted:
  • Brace for Impact
  • Doomed Prophecy
  • Field Dressing
  • Medpack
  • Patch Up
Banned:
  • Drop Off

None of these are a huge shock. Doomed Prophecy wasn’t originally locked to Asgard, and that later change moved it off the Restricted List. Field Dressing and Medpack have since rotated out of Standard play, and Brace and Patch Up remain Restricted.

The banned list has stagnated in recent years because generic cards are much fewer and farther between, and it's largely a non-factor, replaced instead by larger-scale rotations. Cards aren’t banned anymore; they’re simply “rotated out” of the Standard format, which is functionally the same thing.

In hindsight, was introducing a banned and restricted list a good thing? Absolutely, especially paired with another widespread TTC update that we’ll get to later. It did indeed open up rosters to consider a wider variety of cards and stopped games from being dominated by the same 3-4 TTCs every time.

Crisis Selection Revamp 1.0

AMG changed Crisis selection in 2025, but they also changed it much earlier in the game’s life cycle. Originally, players included three Secures and three Extract Crises in their list. Then, after the priority roll, the players randomly discarded one of their own three and manually selected one of the two remaining. This gave players significantly more agency in what they played and functionally meant that you only really had two of each Crisis type in your list if you wanted - players could guarantee that one is never played (either discarded or not selected from the remaining two). Moreover, the priority player also chose the threat level. This gave the priority player plenty of control to “trap” the other player on a Crisis and threat level that best suits them or penalizes their opponent.

The first change shifted this so that Crises would be randomly selected from the full set of three, and the player without priority got to choose the threat. Was this a good change? Absolutely. While the system was later iterated on again, this made it much harder to lock games into the most divisive Crises or threat values (there used to be 14 threat Crises!).

The First Character Update Pass

There are, were, and always will be characters a little above or below average in MCP, but in the early days, it was unclear whether AMG would ever act to rebalance them. The answer came in 2021 when the first batch of updates hit. This pass touched 24 characters, bringing a few up and toning a few others down. The biggest changes include a completely redesigned Hulk, a brand new leadership for Star-Lord, and a threat drop for Bullseye (still the only time a model has changed threat in MCP).

At the time, these changes were billed as a one-time thing to bring earlier designs up to modern standards after the designers had found their footing with the game in players’ hands. That’s obviously proven untrue, and while updates haven’t landed with consistent regularity, the game has seen several subsequent passes, with far more hits than misses.

Infinity Gems Get a Makeover

Infinity Gems remain a powerful and popular element of MCP, but they looked quite different when they were first released. First, they didn’t all “cost” a flat one Threat. The Space Gem had the same effect it does now, but it increased its bearer's threat by 2. The Time Gem got an actual redesign. In its original form, the Time Gem granted an entire additional action! This incredible effect previously cost 2 threat, which still seemed like a bargain for such a wildly impactful bonus. Moreover, Infinity Gems didn’t used to be locked to a character in Roster construction. Instead, they took Roster slots like characters do and could be modularly assigned during Squad building.

Was the change good? Absolutely. I have some qualms about the way locking gems to characters punishes a few bearers, particularly in Black Order, but the homogenization of Threat cost makes sense, and the current Time Gem effect, while perhaps underwhelming, is better than

The First Crisis Set Update & A New Precedent

In the early years of MCP, players could only officially acquire new Crises by purchasing character packs that included them. This was understandably unpopular, as few wanted to purchase models they didn’t want for the Crises their lists needed. AMG eventually moved away from this right around the time of the first Crisis update in 2022. Instead, Crises would be available for purchase but also provided via free online PDFs.

Here, players got one new Crisis (Paranoia Pummels Populace), but it also completely removed single Extracts from the game, replacing their effect with a new one for Crises like Senators and Skrulls. It also brought minor tweaks to Crises like Hammers and Legacy Virus and more substantial ones to SWORD Base. Moreover, it was the death of 14 Threat.

While this wasn’t officially a “rotation,” it set the stage for AMG’s willingness to change Crises for balance or freshness. This didn’t happen again for several years, until the War of Kings rotation in 2025 ushered in a new era of yearly rotation, which continued with Operation: Zero Tolerance in 2026.

Though some lament the decision to remove or not remove certain Crises over the various scenario refreshes, it’s hard to argue against the general concept of rotation (and the removal of Crises from character packs).

In November 2025, AMG dropped several core rules updates at once. The first flattened collision damage. For most of the game’s life, collisions dealt 1+ the size of the terrain or character being thrown. To tone this down, all collisions moved to a flat 3 to be dodged. Did this create some awkwardness in immersion when a small trash can deals as much damage as an entire building being thrown? Sure, but it killed two birds with one stone - it made Brace for Impact much less necessary in every list, and it stopped massive early damage spikes without much counterplay outside said TTC. The downside? Some characters who relied on throw damage felt pretty pillow-fisted. A few have been updated since, but not many. Of all the core rules changes, this remains one of the most divisive.

This update also introduced the second iteration of how Crises are added to Rosters and selected for play. Instead of three Secures and 3 Extracts, the number jumped to five. Instead of randomly drawing, players draw two of their five, and their opponent picks one of those two. The result? You can no longer be forced to play on the one Crisis you like the least. The downside? You’re likely to play the Crisis you like least, and you’ll rarely play your favorite. Like the above, this has proved controversial, and the system may be further iterated in the future. Personally, I’ll take what we have over an older system.

Finally, priority changed. The initial priority roll works the same (though the priority player now chooses threat), but after deployment, a second priority roll determines who takes the first activation. Not knowing who goes first during Squad selection and deployment has gone a long way toward preventing scripted Round 1 plays, though many have been removed from the game anyway. It’s also had a hard-to-measure effect on models who feel best with or without priority. Kraven, for example, thrives when he knows he can go first, so he’s a bit tougher to justify in this new world. Overall, this change has been well received, but it’s hard to judge its effect separately from the gameplay elements that have changed around it.

title: [Kill Team] Tactical Focus: Scout Squad
content:
In this series of Kill Team articles we take a deep dive into one of the available teams, analyzing each team's strengths and weaknesses, how to set up important plays, and ultimately what to consider to pilot the team to victory. Note that this article assumes you already have knowledge of the basic rules for each team, and will reference abilities and ploys from that team throughout. If you want to learn more about the rules for each team you can find the most up to date version of the rules on the Warhammer Community Website here.

The klaxon of your trip alarm signals the enemy presence. New dots light up your auspex screen as you engage your booby trap to slow the oncoming forces. Your Sergeant radios in on the comms, it's time to move out. Readying your shotgun, you relocate to your next position. The enemy is here, engage and eliminate your targets and complete the mission. Will your tactical forward scouting be enough to control the killzone and accomplish your mission or will you and your battle brothers in training find failure in your journey to become Astartes? 

Welcome, dear reader, to our tactical focus on the superhuman war machines-in-training, Scout Squad. The Scouts Squads that make up the various Astartes chapters of the Imperium of Man represent the fresh initiates of the Space Marine ranks, though their bodies are still not yet ready to take the final step into donning the iconic power armor. What they may lack in brawn compared to their elder brothers, though, they make up for plenty in guile, relying on predator cunning to turn any battlefield into a well-laid trap for their foe, overwhelming their opponent before they even know what's going on. Their tabletop incarnation in Kill Team is no different, with a complex but rewarding playstyle that's basically the closest you'll get to putting the A-Team on the board. It's not easy, but learn to master this team and you'll love it when a plan comes together.

Imperial Fist Scouts. Credit: Jack Hunter

In this edition of Tactical Focus, we will teach you how the deep toolbox of Scout Squad and all of their various tricks and traps, how to best pilot their operatives and equipment, and what tactics and teams you need to stay alert for during each game. Let's get right into it then, we've got an ongoing operation to win here, and have got no time to waste.

Overview

Kill Team is a game of careful planning and precise measuring. The Scout Squad kill team personifies this with their Forward Scouting faction rule, allowing them to potentially modify the killzone and their operatives after both players have finished deploying their equipment and operatives. Combine this faction rule with Strategy Phase movement provided by Stealth Relocation and Scouts can exert early pressure on their opponents that can catch players off guard.

Scouts require their pilot to make many pregame decisions, starting with what operatives you want to take. You get a 3 APL Sergeant and eight 2 APL Scouts for your team selection. Aside from your leader who has three optional loadouts, you select the rest of your team from up to five of your specialists and as many of your three warrior variants as you need to fill your remaining spots. This leads to a good variety of team loadouts game to game and always having options for what you are playing into. Nine operatives with a 4+ armor save and 10 wounds on average (your Sergeant is a full fledged Astartes and has 11 wounds) makes you reasonably tough against smaller arms fire, but heavier weapons still remove you from the killzone effectively. 

Credit: Warhammer Community

Strengths and Weaknesses

Your Faction Rule is one of the key strengths of the Scout Squad, understanding what your scouting options do and when to use them is imperative to your success on the killzone. You have nine options to choose from: Relocate, Reposition, Trip Alarm, Booby Trap, Tactical Manoeuvre, Diversion, Devise Plan, Designate Target, and Spy. From that list you can select Trip Alarms and Reposition up to two times. Relocate allows you to redeploy a third of your team. Use this if you make a mistake in your deployment (it does happen from time to time) or use it to show one threat and shift to a different one if your opponent deploys in response to yours. Reposition lets you perform a reposition action but you must finish that action within 3” of your dropzone. Using this in combination with a reposition, dash catapults you up to 12” forward Turning Point 1; who said turn 1 violence was dead? Trip Alarm has you place a marker 6” away from your opponent’s dropzone that grants a 2” radius of Seek. These tokens disappear at the end of Turning Point 2, but while they are in the killzone, they are vital zoning tools that you need to utilize. Remember, you can place these on Vantage terrain or near access points, and keep teams off critical staging points like Volkus Strongholds and Tomb World Doors.

Booby Trap is a little finicky with its placement restrictions, requiring you to place the marker 6” from the opponent’s drop zone, more than 2” from other markers, access points, and accessible terrain then stopping any movement and dealing 2D3 damage. These are best used to shut down approaches from strongholds and lanes where you know they will be going. You can put them in front of light barricades to dissuade enemy charges. If you suspect the opponent’s Tac Op or know it from your Spy scouting option, a mine in their pathway can disrupt an opponent’s otherwise good plan. Devise Plan is simple, 1 free CP. You take Tactical Manoeuvre and Diversion to modify your own APL and your opponent’s APL. Diversion requires the opponent’s operative to be within 6” of a board edge, but you can stop some telegraphed plays or make a first activation play on your opponent’s home objective. Designate Target exists as a source of a reroll in shooting and combat against one target, but there are other options you will want to use more often than this.

Scouts. Credit: Saint

After several rounds of buffs scouts now reliably output enough damage to threaten power armor. Using your Targeting Oculars equipment, Ambush, and Emboldened Aspirant ploys helps confirm critical kills. Scouts killing power shines into 8 wound and lower operatives but do not underestimate their damage output into Elite kill teams with access to a Heavy Bolter,  Missile Launcher, and Sniper operatives. You can also play a little aggressive with the ability to change orders in the strategic phase using Adaptable Training. Scouts excel at scoring double kills into horde teams or double tapping important elite targets, leveraging their Astartes Training firefight ploy which allows them to double fight, double shoot when selecting at least one Bolt weapon, or shoot a second time with one of your gunner operatives for 2 action points. Having the ability to double shoot a Shotgun, Sniper, Heavy Bolter or Missile Launcher threatens damage that every opponent has to respect, especially when you out activate your opponents.

Certain weapon profiles present less than ideal breakpoints. Power Weapons, Plasma Guns, and Meltas all do damage that Scouts do not like to see on the other side of the table. Power Weapons kill them with a crit and a hit. An overcharged Plasma Gun guarantees a kill with 4 normals and a Melta only needs 3 hits to confirm a kill against Scouts. Missile Launchers are threatening and cannot be ignored, but they have a heavy keyword so you can plan for their threat ranges. Against bolters and similar profiles you can often live, especially when paired with your free smoke grenades from your warriors.

Black Templars Scouts. Credit: SRM

Tactics

Capitalizing on your +1 APL buffs is key to success with Scouts. One of the best ways to get the most out of the APL buffs from your Sergeant is to Stealth Relocation forward 3 inches and then reposition shoot shoot, or reposition dash shoot. You can do this in combination with your Targeting Oculars to shoot with a balanced or ceaseless, lethal 5+ Krak Grenades to send a missile on a one way trip for a key target. 

Doing this with your Sergeant and a Tactical Manoeuvre results in a 4 APL beast that can strategy phase dash then move dash 12 inches forward or charge fight fight shoot. You can boost that one inch using a Raw Physiology and ignore injury. Speaking of your Astartes Sergeant, he natively has 3 APL, gives out +1 APL to another Scout in the killzone during his activation, and can shoot or fight twice similar to other Astartes. He acts as the team’s Comms operative and is critical to keep alive to make the team operate at its full output. The Scout Squad kill team has access to +1 APL up to six times a game if your leader stays alive the whole game and you select the Tactical Manoeuvre Forward Scouting option.

Another strategy that utilizes your gunners is to throw a smoke at the feet of your sniper and to use his Optics ability to ignore obscuring and going on guard. While going on guard only works on close quarters maps you can use this same technique on open as your last activation with a regular shoot action. Doing this behind cover with his native camo cloak can make him deceptively tanky.

Using your Hunter for a Krak or Frag Grenade vehicle on Killzone Volkus is a great way to establish asymmetric threats. The Hunter treats the vertical distance of climbs as 2 inches. Use that to climb ruins and strongholds and throw your supercharged Kraks at an operative your opponent mistakenly thought was safe.

Learning when to sit and wait patiently is a skill every Scout Squad player needs to hone to a point. Activating and passing to prevent unnecessary deaths and losing games on Kill Op. Getting behind on Kill Op is easy to do but hard to claw back from.

Scouts. Credit: Corrode

Tac Ops and Crit Ops

Scouts have Infiltration and Recon as their Archetypes. Starting in Infiltration, Track Enemy requires you to throw someone forward within 6” of your opponent, you cannot do this against horde teams or you will be punished so the best time to take this is into teams you out activate and even then you have better options available. Steal Intelligence is effective against teams you are confident you can kill early. Holding one token for three turns nets you 4 points on your tac op; two kills and pick ups nets you 5. Sometimes you’re going to get these chances and this tac op is effective when they come up. Plant Devices is viable into crit ops that require opponents to stay on their home objectives, think Transmission, Orb and Energy Cells.

Moving on to Recon, if you are planning on taking knife or shotgun warriors and pushing forward into the opponent’s territory, Flank can work but will throw operatives forward to likely perish if they do not go first. Your sniper can help you threaten shots and score Scout Enemy Movement. Either your opponent stages the scouted operative out of your vision or they give you easy tac op points. As easy as this sounds to score it can lead to very low scores on your tac op as your opponent can directly influence your score. Retrieval is the Scouts bread and butter. Scouts can reach the opponent’s objective quickly turn 2 with their aforementioned strategic phase dash if they go first and the opponent does not defend against Retrieval. If you do this on your Home and Middle objective you score 4 points very safely as long as you keep those operatives alive. Pairing this with your primary op is a reliable way to score 2 points on primary with you often scoring a 3rd at the cost of a sacrifice.

Scouts appreciate crit ops such as Loot and Stake Claim where you can leverage your bonus APL early on to get ahead on points. For stake claim a trip alarm on the center objective and cover will dissuade most teams from approaching the center point making it easier for you to control. Loot pairs well with Retrieval to move onto an undefended point, loot and retrieve for a 2 Victory Point activation. Repeat that on your home objective and you’ve netted yourself 4 points on two activations.

Match Ups

Scouts like being the controlled aggressor; if you overextend, you will lose too many operatives to be all that effective late in the game. With your 4+ armor save you are going to make some critical saves but you will also miss some of those same saves too. You live by the 4+, you die by the 4+. Scouts thrive into 8 wound teams due to their weapon breakpoints. Anytime you only need two shotgun hits to go through to ensure a kill is a nice time for scouts. Elves, Dwarves and Guardsmen are all prime targets for your shotguns to achieve this. Look for opportunities to set up double kills using your APL boosted warriors in conjunction with your strategy phase dash and Astartes Training double shoot.

Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

Celestian Insidiants are a challenging match up for Scouts; their 3+ save and 9 wound breakpoints make your shotgun math significantly worse. You can reliably trade one for one using your double shoot, but they can riddle you with silent crossbow fire in response. Pair that with their damage reduction in melee combat and Scouts always need 3 hits to kill an Insidiant. 

Marines are still Marines at the end of the day, and they can present a problem match up for Scouts. 3+ power armor and 13+ wounds make Marines tough nuts to crack without using piercing weapons, which Scouts have as well as an activation advantage. However, Marines all have access to innate double shooting or double fighting, so you have to be very careful with your positioning or you can and will lose two Scouts to one Marine fast.

Imperial Fist Scout with auspex. Credit: Jack Hunter

Piloting the Team

Scout Squad’s simplicity is a strength as much as it’s a weakness. You only have five specialists to choose from so the mental load for learning the team is low, but that also means your tricks are easy to learn for your opponent. After selecting which of your specialists you want to take, you need to fill the rest of your team with regular warriors. You can select from warriors equipped with Astartes Shotguns, Bolters or Bolt Pistols and Knives and each turn a warrior can throw one free Stun and Smoke grenade. There are cases for taking each warrior type, with shotguns getting fielded the most. The knife warriors excel at threatening multi kills into horde teams without needing to invest into Astartes Training, although you will likely still bring shotguns as well. Bolter warriors don’t see the field often, but have a niche match up into Vespids due to the break points that bolters hit into 9w operatives. Shotguns are a good take every game. So much of the team’s shooting efficiency comes from your shotguns and you will be happy you have them.

Scouts pressure early to jump out to a lead and hold that until the end. Using your Trip Alarms on the middle objective to exert control over the mid-board is key to approaching this strategy, just be wary of losing too many operatives in doing so. Stage warriors to make runs at the middle and enemy objectives if you are running Retrieval, and stage them to assault the opponent if you are running Steal Intelligence. Your warriors have stun grenades and smokes for free so you can use them to stun the enemy clusters turn 2.

Your specialist operatives each serve a unique purpose on the team. Your Tracker can give your team Seek Light against an enemy within 8 inches of him using his Track Enemy special ability, and use his Auspex Scan to remove obscuring within the same radius. Your Sniper can use his optics rule to ignore obscuring as well, and if he makes a shot against a target under the effects of your Auspex, he gains Seek Light for that shot. Your Heavy Gunners have the Heavy Weapon Bipod special ability, giving them Ceaseless for attacks where they have not moved when they shoot, and Relentless if combined with Ceaseless from Ambush. You won’t take every gunner every game. The Heavy Bolter is great into elites but less effective than a regular shotgun warrior into hordes. The Hunter is fantastic on Volkus for his Lethal 3+ ability that can bully teams in melee. On Tomb World, there are no vantages to run under or drop from, so it is harder to use his special ability.

Imperial Fist Scout with Heavy Bolter. Credit: 40khamslam

Get your points and get out of Dodge! You can reliably take an early points lead at the end of Turning Point 2, but you need to set up with the intention of getting to safety when you activate or through the use of your strategic phase dashes. Getting out to an early lead is doable, but holding it is harder to accomplish if you start to give your opponent too many chances to respond. Only commit what you need to commit for your points. In order to do this effectively comes down to getting the most out of your bonus APL. The primary source of this is your Sergeant and as tempting as using him early to threaten early kills, he can give out up to 4 bonus APL a game to other operatives. Ensuring his safety is paramount to making sure you can buff your other operatives and get the most out of who needs to score you points.

Credit: Warhammer Community

Final Thoughts

Getting the most out of your Scouts requires strategic planning and proactive thinking for where and when you want your operatives to be with their bonus APL. Understanding the tempo of your game, and if you're the aggressor will also dictate when you make your plays. Sometimes the answer is not to just rush the opponent’s home objective with Retrieval, but rather to wait for your opponent to show you what they are planning.

Be wary of over committing your limited resources for low reliability points. It's okay to sacrifice a warrior on the enemy home objective when he can Plant Devices or score you Retrieval. You just cannot lose more than that on your flank. Losing three spread out models is a comfortable spot for scouts to be because your opponent is only at Kill Grade 1, but losing more than one operative on a flank can crush your carefully constructed gameplan.

While Scout Squad can't just overpower most enemy teams with overwhelming numbers or raw muscle, no team offers quite as many ways to alter a battlefield and determine just how a scenario is played quite like them. They reward careful planning, map knowledge, and patient play, and a misstep in any of these can spell disaster. Keep walking on that razors edge without slipping though, and you'll spend most of the game one step ahead of you opponent, forcing them to spend the game on the backfoot while you waltz on in and win.

Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website and more.

title: [Warmachine] The Art of the Team Event, and Overview of the Biggest One of All
content:
In only a matter of days as of this writing, the equivalent of the Warmachine Olympics will begin: The World Team Championship!  The WTC, as it is commonly referred to and will remain so hereafter, is the biggest Warmachine team event in the world.  48 teams of five players from 19 different countries getting together to celebrate the hobby we love... by proving whose country is the best!  WTC lists and results, having the rarity of many of the best players in the world in the same room, get plenty of dissection and this will be discussed, but to zoom out for a moment: How does Warmachine play as a team game?  The answer is: Quite well!  In this article, we will be discussing the general format, process and advantages of running a team event and why it's one of the best ways to play competitive Warmachine even outside of the incomparable community aspect before taking a quick dip into what the world thought was the best in Warmachine this year and why.

The Team Format

Credit: Travis Marg

Team events are typically events of three or five people per team using any combination of armies.  The only composition restriction is that each leader can only be selected once per team, even if the same army appears multiple times within the same team.  Despite the name, the games are all still one-on-one, with the team format used to select team matchups and tables.  This isn't a dual-caster or Unbound event.  Those can be fun, but not what we are discussing here.  Instead, the competitive team format is a matter of opponent and table selection.

After the team captains determine who goes first, one of the teams (Team B) selects one of their players to be "offered" as the initial player.  The other team (Team A) secretly confers and then chooses two of their players to be matched up against the Team B player.  The Team B player then chooses which of the two Team A players they will play against, with the Team A player getting to choose the table the two will play on of those available.

The remaining Team A player, the one that was not picked, will remain and Team B will choose two of their remaining players and offer them to the Team A player, who will then pick their opponent and let Team B choose from the remaining tables.  This process repeats until there is only one player left on each side, who play each other on the final unchosen table.  Once the games begin, the team with more games won wins the round.  In such events, individual team member wins are usually the first tiebreaker, so every game is important even if you know your team has already won or lost the round!

Credit: Steve Rabideau, created for the Bokur Brawl Team Tournament, the largest Warmachine team event in the USA

There can be a lot of calculation and thinking ahead at the high level of matchup selection, but the actual process is fairly simple and it becomes quicker as more players are matched up and fewer remain.

Advantages of the Team Format

Credit: Tried & True

The process of team and table matchup selection may seem complex, but there is a method to the madness.  The specific intricacies of the team event actually lead to some of the best opportunities to play fun and competitive games of Warmachine compared to individual events because of several key factors.

Better Matchups

With the team format, both teams have the opportunity to significantly impact the matchups that are played by offering different armies and players at the right time.  Although this rarely results in a particular team getting to choose a highly favorable matchup, at least without significant consequences for the rest of the team, it does enable most team members to avoid a particular "bad" matchup by not being paired when their bad matchup is offered or simply selecting the other player with the choice of two.  Rather than being fully subject to the vagaries of chance and win rates, this format leads to an overall increase of fair or closer-to-fair matchups throughout the whole event, at least assuming there hasn't been a grave miscalculation!

Greater Army Diversity

Credit: Tried & True

Thanks to the unique leader composition requirements, most teams will have five different armies represented to give the team members unrestricted choices in their army pairings.  This not only encourages lots of different armies at a team event, but the matchup process means that some lesser-used armies that have poor matchups into a particular force have a chance to shine when they can avoid playing against that force entirely.  The broad field also encourages "dark horse" choices in teams where an older or less popular army might be successful thanks to opponent unfamiliarity or bringing a unique mechanic that more popular armies may be unprepared for.  In a particularly large team event like WTC or Bokur Brawl, you have to be prepared for anything!

Terrain That Matters

Credit: Tried & True

Any team event worth its reputation is going to have different tables that emphasize different terrain types, configurations, and otherwise make the "table selection" portion of the team format process meaningful.  Not only does this more closely guarantee relevant table terrain for matches, but also adds another layer to the selection and matchup process.  A player that's matched up against an army of big models may have an easier time dealing with them on a dense table packed with buildings, while a shooty army may be looking for more of a killing field.  The ability to choose tables and actually make them a significant factor in the team selection process means that event organizers can have more freedom to put together tables than a standard singles event.  Many larger team events will have distinct themes for the tables available and many of them are just a joy to look at.

Taking One for the Team (aka The Bus)

For all the control players have, sometimes a player just has to get thrown under the bus.  Sometimes selecting a deliberately bad matchup for one of your players is a necessary strategy to try to ensure that your other matches are as favorable as possible.  Every individual game matters, but ultimately rounds are won and lost as a team and the burden is never solely with an individual.  If a team member got bussed into a bad matchup, made a silly mistake, or simply had a sustained spot of bad dice luck, that's okay.  Even a bad loss can help contribute to a team victory and encouragement and support are built into the format as teams cheer a close loss or laugh off a bad game.  They can be highly competitive, but there's also a sense of shared joy that makes the whole thing more fun, win or lose.

WTC 2026

So now that we know the team format and why team events are so great, let's get into a brief overview of some of the stats for this event.

Popular Armies and Casters

Credit: Steamforged Games

Jumping straight into the deep end here, the single most popular army at WTC is Khador's Old Umbrey at 28 appearances, being the only army to appear on more than half the the team rosters.  Grymkin Wicked Harvest (24), Dusk House Kallyss (23) and Khymaera Shadowflame Shard (20) and Dusk Fane of Nyrro (17) round out the top five.  Fane of Nyrro deserves particular attention as the WTC model cutoff date means that most of the models from Harasheth's "The Gathering Darkness" box are not legal for this event, speaking to Fane's power and popularity even lacking some of their models.  Although these armies are fairly diverse, they highlight an important set of shared qualities.  Namely, all of these armies are melee-focused forces that are capable of either performing fast melee alpha strikes (Shadowflame, Fane, House Kallyss) or tanking up and delivering deadly counterattacks (Grymkin) while simultaneously have powerful defensive effects against shooting.

Old Umbrey can excel at both aspects and it's not surprising that Umbrey's Kazimir Morozov is the most popular leader at WTC at 25 appearances, meaning that only 3 of the 28 Old Umbrey players are not including him in their pairing.  Grymkin's Zevanna Agha and Shadowflame's Lylyth, Raven Vengeance round out the top 3, but honorable mention goes to Kapitan Baranova at 16 appearances within Khador's Winter Korps, whose popularity is clearly intended to stop enemy melee armies in their tracks and who leads one of the two more popular shooting forces (Winter Korps and Gravediggers) appearing on the popular end of the army breakdown.

Low End and Dark Horses

Credit: Steamforged Games

Of the armies that were created since the inception of Mk4, Sea Raiders and Necrofactorium are the lowest at just 10 and 7 appearances, respectively.  Both of these armies have competitive builds, but lack the options and certain quality of life aspects to truly make them popular in the field, or else are being pushed out by the popularity of certain armies that counter them.  Of the print-and-play armies, while Grymkin rule that particular subcategory, a handful of Dark Operations (7), Crucible Guard (6) and Convergence of Cyriss (6) armies are around, each sporting unique mechanics that teams more focused on fighting the mainstream popular choices may not be ready for.  The last print-and-play options are represented by the single solitary Infernals and Thornfall Alliance players, likely speaking to that the Infernals summoning mechanic or Thornfall's new and updated tools are not being highly rated by the current field.

Armies of Legend (armies that are not available to print or buy except via the secondary market) are always interesting to observe.  Soldiers of Fortune and Army of the Western Reaches make 3 appearances each, with the powerful feats and cheap models of Soldiers looking to carry the day while Army of the Western Reaches leverages their powerful beasts and Makeda's Stay Death as an option that not every army can easily answer.  Shadows of the Retribution and Final Interdiction both make 2 appearances as extreme factions that can do quite well in a team event, with Kaelyssa of Shadows asking significantly difficult questions to melee armies while Kreoss's Final Interdiction can be the ultimate answer to questions of defense.  4 other Armies of Legend make single appearances as well, showing that, despite being out of production for at least 5 years now, it's hard to keep a good army down.

Final Thoughts

Credit: Tried & True

The team event is one of the finest ways to play Warmachine that exists and I hope that this article has made a case for why that is.  Even if you don't have much experience, just getting together with a group of people and playing through the day with them is a blast and an experience I'd recommend to anyone who plays the game.  Teams are usually pretty easy to form or even join up with an existing one as a "mercenary" in many events by folks who are happy to shepherd a new team player through the event.

As for WTC, it and the Iron Gauntlet (the game's premier solo event) are considered the annual pinnacles of competitive Warmachine, and for good reason.  Nearly a full year's worth of practice, balance changes, new armies, and events have all led to this, and the analyses of teams, team compositions and individual lists can go into the fine details.  Ironically though, the actual results of these events may not be good predictors of what is strong in the future.  Between the upcoming Covenant of the Flame and Dread Armada armies, the impact of Fane of Nyrro and Thornfall Alliance remaining releases, and the lurking specter of the annual balance update that never fails to shake things up, there's never a time to rest on your laurels.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Historicals: Victrix Early Imperial Roman Range Review
content:
With the recent release of SAGA: Age of Caesars, there are now more options than ever to field various kinds of Roman units. With that in mind, we thought it would be a good time to take a look at the entire range of Imperial Roman miniatures available from Victrix and how to make those kits work for building forces for SAGA.

As mentioned in our recent All the Romans of SAGA article, Studio Tomahawk has finally filled what had previously been a glaring gap in the timeline of warfare in the Mediterranean, Europe, and the Near East. Now, from antiquity all the way up to the fall of Byzantium during the Crusades (and arguably longer if you count the Holy Roman Empire), you can play Romans of some stripe or other in every age the game currently covers.

But usually when people think "Roman," the immediate image that comes to mind is serried ranks of legionaries marching off to do battle with various groups of barbarians, expanding the borders of the Empire and bringing the Pax Romana to the world. That is, when the Empire was at its height, an era that ranges from 52 BCE - when Julius Caesar first led his legions across the Rubicon in defiance of the orders of the Roman Senate - to roughly 300 CE, by which time the Empire had largely split in two and began to be plagued with troubles both internal and external. SAGA: Age of Caesars covers exactly this peak era of the Empire.

Ready and waiting with an impressive range of figures, miniatures manufacturer Victrix Limited offers a number of kits that can have you up and running with a warband for this iconic era right away!

Disclaimer: While Victrix Miniatures often generously provides miniature kits to Tabeltop Battles staff for review, they were not involved with this article. With the exception of the Early Imperial Roman Generals (a spare sprue of which fellow TTB contributor Triphos kindly sent me gratis in the mail), I paid for all of these minis with my own money, largely because I was already in the middle of a massive, ongoing project that dealt with this specific era.

Romans in SAGA

Of the eight factions represented in SAGA: Age of Caesars, three of them (the Caesars' Legions, Imperial Rome, and the Palmyran Empire) can take Legionaries as a core troop type. The Rebels Against Rome faction can take Legionaries as a ruse, while their warriors may be filled with Auxilia. Dacians can take the Manuballista both as a unit and as a ruse, and as mercenary units both the Belgae and the Noble Cavalry could easily be covered by Auxilia and Roman Cavalry figures respectively. As such, unless you're going heavy into camels and cataphracts (looking at you, Bair...), you'll likely be wanting to put at least one unit of "Roman" troops on the table.

Victrix Imperial Romans

In terms of building a force for SAGA, some of the kits are almost "must have" sets, while others are going to have more utility once you are looking to branch out or add some variety to your warband. Let's look at each in more detail.

Early Imperial Roman Legionaries Advancing

These are the troops that come to mind when most people think "Roman Legions," and the kit captures this iconic look in wonderful detail. The kit consists of five infantry sprues, each with four figures. These come as one piece for legs-and-torso, with separate heads (two varieties), shield arms, and weapon arms. There are enough options on each sprue to outfit every soldier with either a leveled pilum (javelin), a shouldered pilum, a pilum used like a walking stick, or a gladius (a short, broad-bladed sword). All of the figures are in various walking/striding poses, but the variations in arm attachment planes and the ability to model a fair amount of turn to the heads can give you impressive variety even for troops who are in very similar poses.

The three options for how the soldiers are holding their pila. There are enough of each option to outfit the entire kit with any one of these, or you can mix and match for variety. (credit: Ilor)

The infantry sprues also include gladii in scabbards. These are a separate piece, so are somewhat small and fiddly. I get why they did this, though, as it gives you the ability to place them on the figure at whatever angle best fits with the arm you happen to be using (see picture above for examples). Finally, each sprue has both square and oval shields, as well as four crests in case you want to outfit your legionaries as Praetorian Guard.

Each legionary soldier is kitted out in lorica segmentata armor, a series of overlapping plates that offered exellent protection against the weapons of the time. This is reflected in the rules, as in SAGA terms legionaries sit between Warriors and Hearthguard, having an Agression of 1, but an Armor of 5. Carrying this hybrid approach even further, they are fielded in units of six for a single point (as opposed to eight or four if they were Warriors or Hearthguard respectively). As such, this kit lets you comfortably build three full points of Legionary troops. That's half of a complete warband from a single kit, which is great!

All twenty legionaries from the Victrix Early Imperial Roman Legionaries Advancing kit completed and ready for battle! Note the mix of swords and javelins, which I did mostly for the sake of variety. (credit: Ilor)

In addition to the legionary sprues, there's a single command sprue with five figures. These are designed to be a Centurion (commander), an Optio (sub-commander), Cornicen (musician), Signifer (unit standard bearer), and Aquilifer (legion standard bearer). If you're playing the Imperial Rome battle board, you're going to want the Centurion at a minimum, as having an extra Hero on the table is key to how that battle board operates. Shockingly, Age of Caesars doesn't include rules for Banners (common to many of the other ages), and aside from the "Wandering Bard" mercenary type in Age of Vikings, has no rules for musicians at all. As such, your other command figures may not see much use in SAGA. That said, with all of the extra heads and arms you certainly could kit them out as regular legionaries if you weren't in need of command figures and didn't mind slight differences in the torso armor. That would allow you to put four full points of Legionaries and a Centurion on the table. 4 1/2 points out of a single kit is a pretty good deal.

From left to right, the Cornicen, Aquilifer, Centurion, Signifer, and Optio. Even though SAGA: Age of Caesars doesn't give you anything special for a standard, multi-basing the Centurion makes him look suitably impressive and clearly marks him out as a Hero on the tabletop. (credit: Ilor)

Early Imperial Roman Legionaries Attacking

If the previous kit seems too staid or static for you, fear not - this kit gives you the same kind of legionaries, only with much more dynamic poses. They likely won't "rank up" as well in small spaces, but for SAGA that's less of a concern than it is in more traditional "rank-and-flank" ancients rules. As such, these are similarly perfect for SAGA.

Once again the kit consists of five infantry sprues, each with four figures, as well as a single command sprue. The command sprue for the attacking Legionaries kit is exactly the same as it is for the advancing Legionaries described above.

The same general method of legs-and-torso with separate heads and arms is carried through here as well, but this time the stances are much more active and dynamic. There's also one notable exception, which is one figure with the legs and torso in two pieces and the cingulum (the little studded leather dangly bits at the front of the belt that were a mark of membership in the legions) as a separate, tiny, extremely fiddly piece. Not sure why they went this particular way, but assemble with care.

Legs-and-torso along with a separate head (left) is a sensible design choice for multi-part miniatures. By contrast, whatever is happening on the right is violence. (credit: Ilor)

The weapon options are similar as well, but this time with a mix of pila and gladii in various stages of throwing/thrusting/striking. Critically, this set completely lacks the optional helmet crests, so if you want to kit out some attacking Praetorians you'll need to steal the crests from the Advancing Legionaries kit.

These miniatures are a little different from the previous kit in that each figure is wearing short trousers underneath their tunics. Once everything is painted and everybody is grouped up on the table I don't think it's overly noticeable, but it's worth mentioning in case you are a stickler for uniformity.

A comparison of the advancing Roman legionaries (left) versus the attacking Roman legionaries (right). I think both look great on the tabletop, and I plan to mix and match them across units, or maybe put the attacking ones in the front rank and the advancing ones in the rear rank. (credit: Ilor)

Early Imperial Roman Auxiliary Infantry

Serving in the Roman military was a path to citizenship in the Empire, and as the Empire expanded it found itself in constant need of soldiers. Those soldiers were formed into units of auxilia, which were often used as light infantry or skirmishers. Trained to fight in the roman style, these troops came from far-flung regions and could reasonably be from pretty much any of the conquered territories.

For SAGA: Age of Caesars, Auxilia are treated as Warriors, fielded in units of 8 men for a single point. The kit consists of seven infantry sprues, each of three men. Regular spears (as opposed to the legionaries' more iconic pila) and gladii are your weapon options, but there are a few flaming brands and trophy heads held aloft are included. That said, the tunic sleeves of the legionaries and auxilia are the same, so you could absolutely raid any legionary sprues you have for additional pila if you wanted to give some to your auxilia. Oval shields are your only option here, but if you're feeling particular savage each infantry sprue comes with sufficient heads and skins to clad each of your auxilia warriors in wolf pelts, as Germanic auxilia are famously depicted on Trajan's column. Scholars debate whether this was an actual military practice or a stylistic sculptural choice, but either way it looks pretty bad-ass.

Much more lightly armored than citizen legionaries, the Roman Auxilia were recruited from throughout the Empire. (credit: Ilor)

Like the legionary kits above, there is a separate command sprue, this time with an additional three figures. There are options for Centurion, Optio, Signifer, and Cornicen, but you'll obviously only be able to build three of them unless you want to dip into your basic soldiers. And like the Legionary kits, you can absolutely just outfit the command figures as regular troops, albeit with better armor. Doing so does let you get a full three points' worth of Warriors out of the kit, though.

Going heavy on auxilia is definitely a viable option, and only auxilia can benefit from the "Gradu Addere" advanced SAGA ability on the Imperial Rome battle board. This ability lets auxilia units perform a Maneuver within L of an enemy, which can be key for early game positioning. Even better, it can be used to allow auxilia units to move farther and (if infantry) ignore the penalties for uneven ground. Combined, this makes auxilia forces extremely speedy. Using "Gradu Addere" to get onto an objective early and then "Circle Up!" to stay there can be an unexpected surprise.

Early Imperial Roman Auxiliary Archers

In the Roman military system, missile troops were also often provided by auxilia units. This kit provides these types of troops for your warband, with 24 figures in the kit. Unlike the archer kits from later ages, this kit is specifically only archers with no option to assemble them as slingers.

Units with missile weapons are typically classed as Levies in SAGA, so having Warriors with bows is an interesting option that can provide for additional resilience and flexibility. (credit: Ilor)

Uniquely, this kit has body and head options for both western and eastern Empire archers, with each of the six sprues having two of each. As such, while the kit as a whole includes 24 archers, if you plan to stick with just one part of the Empire you only get 12.

For me, this 2-and-2 layout is a rare miss from Victrix - I feel like this would probably have been better off as two different sprues/kits. Having both mixed on the same sprue means even if you only want a couple of men (say to round out a second unit of Warriors with missile weapons), you'll need to buy twice as many sprues as you want.

Fortunately, I knew that Bair was planning on building a Palmyran force and could make use of the eastern half of the figures - after I built my half, I sent him the rest of the sprues. Now we both have archers, but it was pure luck that that worked out for us.

This is a little bit of a problem, because you are absolutely going to want at least one 8-man unit of these guys. That's right, in the Imperial Rome faction, Auxilia Archers are classed as Warriors, with an Aggression of 1 in melee and 1/2 in shooting. Without shields they are only Armor 3 and cannot close ranks, but someone charging into the unit and expecting to manhandle them in melee as though they were Levies will be in for an unwelcome surprise. Combined with "Gradu Addere," quickly getting a unit of Auxilia Archers into a terrain piece that provides them with cover is going to make them a pesky inconvenience to your opponent. The Caesars' Legions battle board has less to offer these troops specifically, but the activation efficiency of the "Trained Together" advanced SAGA ability will let you engage in good combined arms play with your archers and your legionary units. Just be aware that for the Caesars' Legions these guys are going to be classed as Levies, so you're going to want 12 of them.

Early Imperial Roman Cavalry

For the Imperial Rome faction, the final option for auxilia is as mounted Warriors, and with 12 figures in the bag this kit lets you field up to 1.5 points of them. The kit contains three rider sprues of four figures each (with a variety of head and weapon options) and three horse sprues of four figures each. While most are clad in chainmail, one of the figures on each rider sprue is wearing scale mail.

It sometimes boggles my mind when I think about it, but when these dudes were riding into battle the stirrup wouldn't be invented for another 800 years. Fighting from horseback seems like it must have been so much harder without stable footing. (credit: Ilor)In this case there is no separate command sprue, and each rider sprue has a couple of standards should you want to equip your troops with them. Again, SAGA: Age of Caesars doesn't allow banners, but sometimes looking cool is what you've got to do.

Fellow TTB Historicals contributors Bair and Mugginns always give me crap about my goofy basing scheme for horses, but it lets me use the same sabot bases for both infantry and cavalry. (credit: Ilor)

My love of painting horses is well-established, and these guys were a lot of fun to build and paint. I can't wait to field them in a game. Clever deployment, a mounted Warlord, and timely use of both "Gradu Addere" and "Rest Halt" could allow you to pull off a rare Turn 1 charge with no fatigue - surprise! These figures would also work perfectly as non-cataphract mounted Warriors for several of the other factions, or even as "Noble Cavalry" mercenaries.

Early Imperial Roman Mounted Generals

The kit gives you a bunch of different options, but I chose to do a mounted version of the Centurion from the Legionaries kit I had already finished. I think the next one will be an older, patrician-looking dude suitable for one of the command options in the Caesar's Legions warband. (credit: Ilor)

I'm going to be honest, this kit mystifies me a little bit. Like the cavalry this kit includes 12 figures, but it's four copies of the same sprue (each of which has three horses and three riders). But am I ever going to need 12 generals? The only thing I can think of is that you'd build maybe one or two generals from this kit, then raid the Early Imperial Roman Cavalry kit described above for extra heads or spears, giving you the ability to field more cavalry units. But apart from that, having a full dozen of these particular figures seems like overkill. If you have access to a "buy-by-the-sprue" service (or have some friends you can go in with together), I would probably recommend that.

That said, these figures are great. Especially if you are playing the Caesars' Legions battle board, all three of your Warlord options (Consul, Tribune, and Legate) have the option to be fielded mounted. This kit is perfect for those roles, and with a single sprue you could do a unique option for all three.

Early Imperial Roman Bolt-Shooters

When you absolutely, positively need to drive a spear through someone's chest at long range, Roman artillery perfected the process with the ballista. Harnessing the power of tension and torque, these fearsome weapons provided long range firepower capable of damaging even heavily armored targets.

This set lets you bring that terrifying artillery engine to the tabletop. The kit consists of four identical sprues, each with enough parts to build the ballista itself (with options for both uncocked and ready-to-fire configurations) and four legionary crew members. Like the attacking legionary kit, there is one guy on the sprue with the separate torso - and the separate cingulum - again. Brutal.

In terms of arm/weapon options, there are a couple of swords and pila, but also a number of axes and splitting mauls, as well as a couple of buckets. Better yet, there are arms that can be hooked to the windlass handle to model your ballista in the process of being wound/loaded.

Tension-driven weapons like the ballista deliver a terrifying amount of force. The rate of fire isn't high, but the range and potential impact they offer convinced many a Roman general that they were worth lugging into the field. (credit: Ilor)

SAGA: Age of Caesars treats these as the "Manuballista," a unique weapon whose Aggression score in shooting is based on the number of figures in the target unit. As a result the size of the weapon's crew doesn't matter, as it tracks its current "health" through Fatigue (the unit is considered a single model which has the "Resilience" rule), so a single sprue gets you a complete unit. Putting one into your warband costs just a half-point. Sadly, in this Age you can only ever field a single Manuballista (although as a ruse the Dacians can field a second one). As such, like the mounted generals you might want to split this kit with a friend.

Each sprue also contains a couple of terrain items like a barrel and a bunch of defensive stakes. These could absolutely be used to make some nice barricades, such as you might need if you use the "Tribuli" ruse from the Caesars' Legions warband.

Imperial Rome Warband

This is a recent release from Victrix and seems to be a direct response to the release of SAGA: Age of Caesars. Like the other warband kits released to support Victrix' own Pillage wargame, this set combines sprues from other kits. In this case, the warband includes four Advancing Legionary sprues, four Attacking Legionary sprues, one Legionary Command sprue, and a single Bolt Shooter sprue, a total of 41 figures and a ballista for $69. That's a hell of a bargain!

If you treat one of the command figures as your leader and another as a Centurion, that's a complete 6-point warband with:

  • Warlord
  • Centurion (0.5 points)
  • Manuballista (0.5 points)
  • 5x 6-man Legionary units (5 points)

What it lacks in variety it's going to more than make up for in brutal order efficiency and damage-soaking resilience. And the fact that it's a complete, legal, 6-point force in a single bag is pretty amazing. Fellow TTB contributor Hydriatus wrote a really nice review and "How to Paint Everything" article for this kit last week (check it out!), and it serves as a great entry point for someone wanting to get into the period.

Decisions, Decisions...

If you are looking to jump into SAGA: Age of Caesars - and you should, it's awesome! - having some legionaries or auxiliaries on hand is almost certainly worth doing. Though you'll get the most use out of them with the Caesars' Legions and Imperial Rome battle boards, they can serve as a nice way to branch out into other boards like the Palmyrans or Rebels Against Rome. Some of the kits are more niche (bolt throwers and generals in particular), but give you additional flexibility when building your list. Getting individual sprues for these would be ideal, but if your gaming group is getting into the game together then chances are good you'll be splitting them up among your buddies anyway.

Further, while by the end of the 4th century the Roman Legions and largely exchanged the large, rectangular scutum shield for a smaller, lighter oval design and moved from the short-bladed gladius to the longer spatha, you could easily put together a warband using these figures along with the Romans board from SAGA: Age of Invasions and everything would be immediately recognizable (including the manuballista, which is still an option in the later age).

If you have any interest whatsoever in wargaming during the age of antiquity - whether SAGA or some other game system - chances are good you're going to need Roman legions at some point. Now you'll have a better idea of your options!

If you want to get some Victrix kits of your own, please consider using our affiliate link for your purchase. It doesn't cost you anything and it helps us continue covering the games and kits that we love! Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: MTG's K Pop Demon Hunters Secret Lair is overshadowed by a bunch of hippy treefolk
content:
K-Pop Demon Hunters may be last year's big thing, but that still makes it two decades more current than most of the brands Wizards of the Coast has worked into Magic the Gathering via the Universes Beyond initiative. Unfortunate, then, that 'Secret Lair X K Pop Demon Hunters: That's How It's Done' is among the weaker offerings in the latest round of Secret Lair reveals.

 

The Lair consists of seven cards, and card count is the only domain in which it's above average. All seven are reprints of existing Magic cards, and all seven feature recycled art. It's very good art, production art from K Pop Demon Hunters by freelance development artist Scott Watanabe and production designer Helen Chen, as well as one piece that is only credited to Netflix. But the only original creativity in the product is the choice of which cards to stick to which art - the branded lunch box of Secret Lairs.

1/7

Weirdly for a franchise with such big characters, none of the cards is a creature. The absence of cards for each member of HUNTR/X feels like a really odd omission. The one upside I can suggest for K Pop Demon Hunters fans is that perhaps this omission is a sign that there'll be another lair in the future - maybe with original card designs? But it's not here now.

The lair also isn't packed with high value reprints. Going off market prices on MTG Goldfish, you could buy all the cards in the basic $29.99 version of the Secret Lair for $36. Swan Song, Dawn's Truce, Freed from the Real, and Underworld Breach all see decent play in a few formats and make up the bulk of the value, but they're not so rare as to be bank-breakers. I must acknowledge that the cards in the $39.99 foil Secret Lair are worth around $100, $60 of that from the foil Swan Song, which has precious few printings.

Nevertheless, if the goal is to make a good first impression for the franchise, How It's Done isn't how it's done,. It's not a tonal mismatch on the level of the delayed Monster Hunter Secret Lair, but it does feel like a minimum viable product. As an adaptation of an existing IP, it compares poorly to the lavish Labyrinth Secret Lairs revealed in this drop. And in both artistic terms and value for money, it's greatly outdone by Secret Lair: Peace, Love, & Treefolk, which I'm mentioning because it's such an oddball.

Peace, Love, & Treefolk is the least expected Secret Lair in this drop, a selection of five Treefolk first printed in the original Lorwyn block. All five are illustrated by Ashley Dreyfus in an art style I can only call "1970s psychedelic children's book", making this an Artist's Series drop by another name. And having scarcely been reprinted since they first appeared in Lorwyn, the regular version five cards currently have a total market price of around $50, while the foil versions are again worth around $100. And something I always look for when judging a lair - the strong typal theme makes it obvious that you could run all five of these cards in the same deck.

What do you think? Are you going to grab any of these Lairs? Which legendary creatures do you think would make good stand-ins for the members of HUNTR/X? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: All MTG sets in order, as of October 2026
content:
Over the game's 33-year history, Wizards of the Coast has released 233 card collections, better known as MTG sets. With thousands of cards behind us, and even more approaching, that's a lot of sets to track. To help you stay up-to-date, we've put together a complete list of all Magic: The Gathering sets in order.

Because everybody wants to know what's new, we start with the up-and-comers and the most recent sets released. After that, our total of 233 counts all Core, Standard Expansion, Supplemental, Starter, Compilation sets since 1993, as well as the jokey 'Un-Sets', one-and-done Box Sets, Commander Sets, and miscellaneous multiplayer products.

Since Commander is such a big part of the game, we've also copied out all the Commander precons and other commander products into a separate list . We haven't counted digital-only Alchemy sets, but there are some MTGO exclusive sets in here!

For info on just the latest sets, you can find more drilled-down detail in our MTG release schedule guide. You can also hop to our FAQ segment below for some helpful facts and trivia about the history of Magic: The Gathering sets.

MTG Commander sets

From 2011 to 2019, Wizards of the Coast released Commander decks and other products just once per year. Since May 15 2020, the firm has released batches of precons parallel to new mainline Magic sets. Although they share the set's theme and narrative, they have their own set code and set symbol.

Starting with Theros: Beyond Death in January 2020, Wizards started putting cards from these Commander sets in the main set's Collector or Set boosters. To make things more confusing, some cards in certain Commander sets could only be found in the (non-draftable) boosters for the main set, and not in the accompanying precons.

As of June 2026, there have been three draftable Commander sets sold in booster packs:  Commander Legends, Battle for Baldur's Gate, and Commander Masters. All three of these sets came with Commander precons, but the draft cards and the precons all shared the same set code and set symbol.

The Doctor Who and Fallout Universes Beyond Commander sets also had Collector Boosters. These contained alternate art treatment versions of cards found in the precons.
