Magic: The Gathering sets FAQ

Above are all the sets, right back to the very beginnings of Magic: The Gathering, but if you're new to the game, some more info might be in order. Here's the lowdown on how these releases work.

What are MTG sets?

Most Magic: The Gathering sets aren't individual boxed products on a shelf, like Lego sets or Warhammer 40k box sets. Instead, an MTG set is a distinct, named new collection of MTG cards released and added to the game's existing pool of playable cards.

Depending on the type, each set will normally have its own theme, either based around a particular fictional setting in the lore, or perhaps tailored to one particular mode of play, like the Commander or Modern formats.

What are the types of MTG sets?

We've created several categories to make our list of every MTG set easier to peruse. Here's what those terms mean:

  • Expansion: These are the regular Magic: The Gathering sets, legal in Standard, and released at regular intervals throughout the year.
  • Compilation: These are reprint sets with no new cards. Often these contain a compilation of cards set on the same plane.
  • Un-set: These are joke sets with cards that have weird, wacky effects. Cards from these sets usually have silver borders and are not been legal in other formats.
  • Universes Beyond set: One of Magic: The Gathering's many crossover sets. Now that MTG Universes Beyond sets are Standard-legal, this category has merged with regular expansions somewhat.
  • Core set: Beginner-friendly sets that are Standard legal - these have been canceled and reintroduced several times.
  • Box set: Sets with a predetermined batch of cards, where what you get is not randomized.
  • Supplemental set: A catch-all category for MTG sets that don't fall into one of the above categories. These include many of WotC's experiments over the years, as well as expansions built for specific formats other than Standard.

When do new MTG sets come out on MTG Arena?

Currently, every new Standard set releases on MTG Arena a few days before the physical products are available in stores. 

Most new Standard sets also herald an Alchemy release of about 25-30 Arena-only cards that are not produced in physical form. These cards are specially designed to work best in the digital format. They often include mechanics that would be impractical in regular Magic, such as summoning random creatures from your deck, creating new cards, or permanently altering others.

Are Universes Beyond sets also released on MTG Arena?

As of June 2026, two of Wizards of the Coast's Universes Beyond crossover sets have been released in digital form on MTG Arena: the mighty, best-selling MTG Lord of the Rings and MTG Final Fantasy sets.

Now that Universes Beyond sets are Standard-legal, and have even lost the distinctive card borders that separated them from regular cards, Universes Beyond sets are also released on MTG Arena (and MTG Online).

Not every UB set is making a smooth transition to digital platforms, however. On April 21, 2025, Wizards announced 'Through the Omenpaths' sets, Magic versions of non-Magic Magic sets (confused yet?) Presumably due to a wrinkle in the licensing deal with Marvel, Wizards is creating reskinned in-universe versions of all Marvel Spiderman cards for its online platforms.

This is the form in which these cards will make it to MTG Arena and MTG Online. All Marvel sets going forward are going to receive this treatment.

How many cards are in each MTG set?

Each new MTG set normally contains somewhere between 200 and 300 cards. The selection almost always includes a mixture of brand new cards (where the card name, in-game rules, and art are all new) and 'reprints' (new versions of existing popular cards, which keep the same name and rules, but may feature new artwork and sometimes updated wording).

What is the biggest MTG set ever released?

The biggest single MTG set ever released was the Fifth Edition core set in 1997, which had 449 new cards in total, including 20 Basic Lands.

Other massive sets from the early era of Magic include its immediate predecessor, 1995's Fourth Edition core set, with 363 cards; 1996's Mirage, with 350, and 1997's Tempest, which also added 350 cards to the game.

Sets started becoming smaller during the aughts, although 2007's  Lorwyn bucked the trend with a mighty 301 cards.

What is the smallest MTG set ever released?

The smallest MTG set of all time, by total number of cards, is technically 2023's March of the Machine: Aftermath, with just 50 new cards. But, if we discount that as merely a mini add-on to the 291-card March of the Machine, the smallest legitimate set is Arabian Nights, the very first 'expansion' set, released in December 1993 with just 92 cards.

Oh, you meant the actual smallest cards? That honor is held by the Worlds Smallest Magic: The Gathering Exclusive Collector Set pictured above - a painfully adorable, now sadly discontinued joke product that included two itsy-bitsy duel decks composed of downsized, 1.2 x 1.8 inch cards, as well as teeny weeny spindown dice.

How many MTG sets are released each year?

Currently, Wizards of the Coast releases between six and ten MTG sets per year. We get three to four full 'Standard' sets annually (about one every three months) and a varying mix of smaller sets - usually focused on specific formats, or revisiting a popular past setting with additional cards.

According to comments from Magic's head designer Mark Rosewater in May 2026, the "new normal" from next year onwards will be a "three and three" split between Universes Beyond crossover sets (like Lord of the Rings and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles) and sets based in Magic's own fiction (like Lorwyn Eclipsed and  Secrets of Strixhaven).

In addition, Wizards releases what it calls 'Secret Lair drops', which are much smaller, limited edition print runs of specially designed cards aimed at collectors - often themed around franchises, fandoms, or art styles outside of Magic.

What products come with each MTG set?

Every time a new MTG set is released, Wizards of the Coast produces a range of different products containing the new cards, in different configurations, for various types of players.

Currently, every main MTG set releases with:

  • Play boosters - packs of 14 random cards including at least one Rare or Mythic Rare.
  • Collector boosters - packs of 15 random cards including 4-5 guaranteed Rares and Mythic Rares, plus special art cards.
  • Bundles - a mixed box containing 9 play boosters, 30 land cards, and accessories like tokens and counters.
  • Commander decks - pre-built 100-card decks for the Commander (EDH) game format. Each set normally has between two and four of these, also called Commander 'precons' (short for preconstructed decks).
  • Prerelease pack - A box sold at prerelease events, with six Play boosters, one promo card (a foil Rare or Mythic Rare stamped with the year), a deck box, an Arena code, and a spindown die with the set symbol.

What are the most popular MTG sets?

The answer depends a lot on personal taste, but there is a way to generally feel out which sets are most loved - and that's money. According to Hasbro, the best-selling MTG set of all time is Final Fantasy. Second and third place also go to Universes Beyond sets, with MTG Lord of the Rings following Final Fantasy, and Avatar: The Last Airbender bringing up the rear.

If you'd like to debate which of these sets is truly best, you've got a willing audience over in the Wargamer Discord - and to stay informed about upcoming releases, subscribe to the Wargamer newsletter.

title: MTG Arena codes for October 2026
content:
MTG Arena codes are an essential, mostly free kick-start for your digital collection, unlocking new Magic: The Gathering cards, booster packs, XP, and cosmetic items like card sleeves, avatars, and more. Read on to find all working MTGA codes in 2026, as well as full instructions on how to redeem promo codes on PC and mobile.

Each month, we trawl Wizards' announcements about new MTG sets to update this list (if you want more details on said sets, check out the linked guide, or this one on the MTG release schedule). We'll tell you which codes currently work; which have expired; and which brand-new codes have sprung up for the game. The good news is that you can still unlock free cards to boost your decks.

Here's how to get MTGA codes:

  • All free MTG Arena codes in October 2026
  • Unlock the cabbage companion
  • MTG Arena rewards
  • How to redeem MTG Arena codes
  • Where to find more MTGA codes
  • All expired MTGA codes

All free MTG Arena codes in October 2026

For the first time in ages, there actually are MTG Arena codes to be used (for now, at least!) A chain of riddles, released alongside the Hobbit set, will win you some cards, card styles and a unique avatar.

Originally, this promo was expected to end around August 27, but as of our latest test on Tuesday, October 1, it still works! We can't be sure how long for, though, so if you want your Bilbo goodies, hurry up! Here's what to do:

Right now, if you check your inbox, you'll find a riddle. Input the answer as an MTG Arena code in the store to unlock a reward and the next riddle. Keep going until you've answered all eight, then create a deck with all eight of the cards you just unlocked. 

It doesn't have to be legal, or even have the correct number of cards, so just plonk them all in and save it. Name the deck 'Riddles in the Dark', and you'll receive a Bilbo avatar.

If you want to try to solve the riddles yourself, exit this page right now. We're assuming you're here for the answers, which you'll find below.

  • Riddle #1: Mountain (The Mountain-king's Return card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #2: Teeth (Gnashing of Teeth card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #3: Wind (Velvetwing Butterflies card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #4: Darkness (Gathering of Darkness card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #5: Egg (Well-Worn Spatula card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #6: Fish (Lake-town Mariners card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #7: Time (Stone by Sunlight card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #8: Precious (My Precious rare card and borderless card style)

In case you skimmed the bit above, you now need to make a deck called Riddles in the Dark with all eight of these cards to unlock the final reward.

Unlock the cabbage companion

Would you like to have a high fidelity cabbage for your companion? Of course you would! This nutritious friend is available as a free easter egg, added to celebrate the MTG Avatar: The Last Airbender set in 2025. You can unlock it by playing any matched game on the Avatar battlefield, and clicking on the Cabbage Merchant's cart until it explodes. Do this and you'll be rewarded with your very own cabbage.

Can't find the cart? It's at the top of the battlefield, just to the left of your opponent's profile picture.

Is the cabbage companion better than the beachball or the pet rock? That's for you to judge.

MTG Arena rewards

These days, Wizards hands out free booster packs as MTG Arena rewards to celebrate the release of new sets. These arrive directly in your in-game inbox without the need to redeem a code. Plus, new players who complete the how to play tutorial are greeted with a whole stack of reward packs to crack open from the last couple of years' worth of sets (plus a selection of variant land cards to use).

Here are all the rewards each MTG Arena player has access to, as of October 2026:

  • 3 x Alchemy: Strixhaven boosters
  • 3 x Secrets of Strixhaven boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Lorwyn boosters
  • 3 x Lorwyn: Eclipsed boosters
  • 3 x Avatar: The Last Airbender boosters
  • 3 x Through the Omenpaths boosters
  • 3 x Edge of Eternities boosters
  • 3 x Magic: The Gathering - Final Fantasy boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Tarkir boosters
  • 3 x Tarkir: Dragonstorm boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Aetherdrift boosters
  • 3 x Aetherdrift boosters
  • 3 x MTG Foundations boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Duskmourn boosters
  • 3 x Duskmourn boosters
  • 3 x Bloomburrow boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Bloomburrow boosters
  • 3 x Modern Horizons 3 boosters
  • 3 x Lost Caverns of Ixalan boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Ixalan boosters
  • 3 x Murders at Karlov Manor boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Karlov Manor boosters
  • 3 x Shadows Over Innistrad Remastered boosters
  • 3 x Phyrexia: All Will Be One boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Phyrexia boosters
  • 3 x Outlaws of Thunder Junction boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Thunder Junction boosters
  • 3 x The Lord of the Rings: Tales of Middle-earth boosters
  • 3 x Wilds of Eldraine boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Eldraine boosters
  • 3 x Khans of Tarkir boosters
  • 3 x March of the Machine boosters
  • 3 x March of the Machine: The Aftermath boosters
  • 1 x Basic Wastes Land (from Explorer Anthology 2)
  • 6 x Alchemy: Brothers War boosters

How to redeem MTG Arena codes

There are two ways to redeem MTG Arena codes on PC, and both are dead easy - just pick your method below and follow our step-by-step guide.

How to redeem codes in the Arena client

The most common and simplest way to cash in your codes is directly inside the MTG Arena client. Here's how to do it:

1. Open up the game on PC and click on the 'Store' tab at the top of the page.

2. You'll see a small oval text box in the top right corner, with 'Redeem Code' written inside (we've highlighted it in red in the picture above).

3. Copy your code into the box and hit enter.

4. Your reward automatically appears in your account!

How to redeem codes via your Wizards account

If you'd rather not boot up the game, you can also redeem codes by entering them into your Wizards of the Coast account page. Here's how you do this:

1. Log in using your MTG Arena details, and on the right-hand side of your account dashboard, you'll find a nice, big 'Redeem a code' box.

2. Paste the code inside and click 'Redeem'.

3. The goods will appear in your account next time you log in to the Arena game client.

How to redeem MTGA codes on mobile

If you're primarily a mobile MTGA player and want to redeem codes on your phone, the process can feel a bit more convoluted, because - frustratingly - there's still no way to redeem codes directly through the iOS and Android versions of the game.

The main way to get the job done is simply via mobile web, with the following steps:

  1. Log in to your Wizards account via your mobile browser.
  2. Scroll down to the 'Redeem a Code' box as shown in the image above.
  3. Enter your code, and click 'Redeem'.
  4. Your rewards will show up next time you log into the game.

If everything's worked correctly, you'll see a little green message pop up that reads "Code redeemed successfully", as seen above.

However, if you really want to make things difficult for yourself, you can access that same account-based process from within the MTG Arena mobile client. We don't recommend it, though, because it's janky as all hell - it's far easier just to hop over to your mobile browser and do it there.

Where to find more MTGA codes

If you've already used all the free codes available, and still want to expand your collection of planeswalkers, creatures, and fancy land cosmetics, there are a few other places where you can sometimes get your hands on more MTGA codes to redeem. You can do this either by buying select Magic products that include Arena freebies, or else staying alert for new promo codes and other fans' unused codes shared online.

The main options to try are:

  • Physical Magic: The Gathering products
  • Social media giveaways and competitions
  • Promo codes from local game stores
  • MTG Arena Twitch Prime codes

Physical Magic: The Gathering products

Unlike the Pokémon TCG, not every sealed pack of Magic cards comes with a digital unlock code included - but some physical MTG products do give you a code into the bargain, to grow your digital collection as well as your cardboard mountain. There are three types of products you can buy for this.

Prerelease kits

Wizards of the Coast launches each new Magic: The Gathering set with a pre-release event focused on in-person games in local game stores, selling Prerelease kits of six brand new boosters.

Since 2025, these prerelease kits have no longer included MTG Arena codes packed in the box. Instead, you'll register your Arena account when you attend the pre-release event at a physical store, and your free boosters will appear in your account when you next log in.

However, older prerelease kits can still be found for sale which do contain Arena codes. If you buy one of the following recent Prerelease kits, you can use the included code to unlock MTG Arena boosters for the corresponding set:

Product Reward Approx. Price Link
Murders at Karlov Manor Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters  $30 Buy at Amazon
Lost Caverns of Ixalan Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters  $30 Buy at Amazon
Outlaws of Thunder Junction Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters  $30 Buy at Amazon 
Commander Legends: Battle for Baldur's Gate Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters $47 Buy at Amazon
Kaldheim Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters $32 Buy at Amazon
Ikoria Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters $56 Buy at Amazon
Zendikar Rising Prelease kit 6 Arena boosters $27 Buy at Amazon

Starter kits

Starter kits are designed to get newbies into Magic: The Gathering, so they offer up two pre-constructed decks. The kits also come with a code that unlocks each deck in MTG Arena, too.

Buying a second-hand starter kit might mean that your code has already been used, but if you can get one new (or from a reputable, code-selling source), these are the decks to look out for:

  • Bloomburrow Starter Kit
  • Wilds of Eldraine Starter Kit
  • Lord of the Rings Starter Kit
  • Starter Kit 2023
  • Starter Kit 2022
  • Starter Kit 2021
  • Core Set Starter Kit 2021

Planeswalker decks

All physical Planeswalker decks released between the October 2018 set Guilds of Ravnica and Core Set 2021 came with a one-time code to unlock their cards in MTG Arena, so you could use all the same cards online.

Sadly, the older codes from these decks have now expired, and the decks themselves are very difficult to come by (they're all unavailable on Amazon US and UK) - so you'll struggle to find an unopened copy with an intact code for a reasonable price. Even more sadly, free codes isn't a trend that was carried on by the far more available Commander precons.

If you really want the physical cards too, though, it might be worth the hunt; here's the full list of decks with (we think) still functioning codes:

  • Ashiok, Shaper of Fears
  • Basri, Devoted Paladin
  • Chandra, Flame's Catalyst
  • Elspeth, Undaunted Hero
  • Liliana, Death Mage
  • Oko, The Trickster Planeswalker
  • Rowan, Fearless Sparkmage
  • Teferi, Timeless Voyager
  • Vivien's Hunt (released in a Hot Pocket promo)

MTG Arena Secret Lair codes

MTG Arena Secret Lair codes are found in Wizards of the Coast's limited edition, premium Secret Lair boxed sets of one-off collectible cards. The rewards vary, but usually, they unlock exclusive cards and cosmetics.

You can get some pretty sweet, limited edition skins, though - for example, if you bought the 'Warhammer Bundle' during the October 2023 Warhammer 40k Secret Lair, you got two codes, each good for ten premium card sleeves showing the 40k-ified versions of classic cards:

  • Merciless Executioner as "Ork Kommando"
  • Aggravated Assault
  • Krenko, Tin Street Kingpin as "Makari the Lucky Grot"
  • Zurgo Helmsmasher as "Ghazghkull, Prophet of the Waaagh!"
  • Blind Obedience
  • Danitha Capashen, Paragon as "Neave Blacktalon"
  • Najeela, the Blade-Blossom as "Archaeon the Everchosen"
  • Scourge of the Throne as "Stardrake"

Beware, though - this is often the priciest way to find new codes. Each Secret Lair 'drop' can cost anything from $20 to several hundred bucks. We only recommend going this way if you really want the physical cards your codes will come bundled with.

Social media giveaways and competitions

If you're a social media-savvy Magic fan, another way to nab a cheeky extra code is through giveaways or competitions run by major MTG content creators, influencers, or simply kind-hearted fans sharing codes they don't need or want for themselves.

MTGA Codes, a retail website that collects unwanted and unused Arena codes and sells them directly online, regularly runs such giveaways to drive engagement on its Twitter account (@MTGA_CODES).

There's no way to know when such giveaways will take place, or exactly who's going to be doing them - but we can recommend a few creators you should follow just for regular, great content and commentary on Magic and Arena, who have been known to give away MTGA codes in the past:

  • Grzegorz 'Urlich' Kowalski (@urlichmtg) - former Magic Pro League player, Twitch streamer
  • Gerry Thompson (@G3RRYT) - Magic pro player from the US
  • The Asian Avenger (@Theasianavenger) - Magic YouTuber and streamer
  • MTGNerdGirl (@MTGNerdGirl) - Magic YouTuber and streamer

Promo codes from local game stores

It's not all the time, but Wizards of the Coast occasionally creates special MTG Arena codes as part of promoting in-person Magic play through bricks-and-mortar local game stores (LGS). Most recently, it did this via its 'Friday Night Magic At Home' campaign, aimed at helping stores keep regular play events going during Covid lockdowns in 2020.

This isn't a regular occurrence, though, and it's entirely dependent on Wizards' ongoing strategy for working with game stores - if you're angling for extra codes, we'd recommend checking in with the staff at your LGS to see if there's anything on offer.

MTG Arena Twitch Prime codes

In the past, Wizards of the Coast has collaborated with other big brands to offer MTG Arena promo codes as a bonus for their subscribers - and, back in 2019, it gave away free unlock codes as a benefit for the Twitch Prime service (now merged with Amazon Prime Gaming).

All you had to do to get the code was sign into your Twitch Prime account, check the 'Loot' section, click on 'claim', and it would generate a code for you to redeem directly in the Arena client.

Sadly, we haven't seen any more new MTGA codes come through this service in the years since - but there's always a chance, so if you're constantly on the hunt for fresh codes, it's worth periodically checking in on your Prime Gaming account (there's also a bunch of free videogame downloads and other goodies there, of course).

Naturally, we'll also update this guide the moment we see any new MTG Arena unlockables pop up on the platform.

Expired MTG Arena codes

Wizards don't set these codes up to work forever, and (as we said) might be phasing them out altogether. The following expired MTG Arena codes are already dead and gone - if you try to redeem them, you'll get a sad little red error message that reads: "This code is not valid or has already been used the maximum number of times for this account".

Expired special or puzzle codes

From February 2024 to February 2025, MTG Arena players could use a specific method to claim a free unique cosmetic and XP bonus. Wizards gave the freebies away as the reward for an ARG hidden in various products and marketing for the Murders at Karlov Manor set.

Code Reward Expiration date
thewayisopen (see Karlov Manor code instructions above) 5,000 XP and MKM card sleeves February 6, 2025

Sadly, the promotion ended on Thursday, February 6, 2025 - so you can no longer use this method to get the rewards. However, it's still worth understanding how it worked, as it could help us piece the clues together quicker, should Wizards run a similar secret promo in future.

Here's how you claimed the Karlov Manor 'thewayisopen' code:

  1. First, you had to create a deck that includes these cards:
  • 1 Extract a Confession
  • 1 Homicide Investigator
  • 1 Leering Onlooker
  • 1 Glint Weaver
  • 1 Granite Witness
  • 1 Meddling Youths
  • 1 Furtive Courier
  • 1 Case of the Stashed Skeleton
  • 1 Out Cold
  • 1 The Pride of Hull Clade
  • 1 Reckless Detective
  • 1 Novice Inspector

You didn't have to actually own the cards or craft them for the hack to work.

2. You had to name your new deck 'thewayisopen' (don't worry that it's 'invalid' for play).

3. Done! At this point, you automatically received 5000 XP and the exclusive card sleeves.

If you've found a new working code we've missed (or just want to come share your favorite MTGA cards, combos, and decks right now) join the free Wargamer Discord community and let us know! It's the best tabletop games server there is, with chats going on daily, regular live AMAs from game designers, giveaways, hobby hangouts, and more. Or subscribe to the Wargamer newsletter to keep up to date with the latest news and features about MtG and everything else tabletop.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Blood Brothers Auxilia
content:
In this series of articles we take a deep dive into a specific detachment for a faction, covering the faction’s rules and upgrades and talking about how to build around that faction for competitive play. In this article, we’re covering the Brood Brothers Auxilia Detachment for Genestealer Cults. 

Brood Brothers is one of the most talked about lore sub factions for Genestealer Cults, but unfortunately their recent rules set in the GSC Codex hasn’t lived up to that hype.

Detachment Cost: 2 DP

Force Disposition: Take and Hold

While I’m not the biggest fan of Brood Brothers as a Detachment in this Codex, I will say I think that Take and Hold is one of the better dispositions you could run for this army. Between two armies you have some of the cheapest 20 man units you could find so just having a list that is an Objective Control stat check with a bunch of bodies that just sit and hold points then T&H is your spot to be.

Detachment Rule: Brood Brothers

To short hand the allies part, you can include up to 1000 points of Astra Militarum units in the list but none of them can be your Warlord and you can’t include Aircraft, Commissar, Epic Hero, Militarum Tempstus, Ogryn, Ratling, Tech-Priest Enginseer, and Ministorum Priest units. It is also worth noting that your army rule is still Cult Ambush not Voice of Command so you don’t get access to orders outside of units that can specifically order themselves like Kasrkin. This is a fine part and basically what we’ve seen for most “soup” Detachments in the 10th edition codices. I normally wouldn’t recommend 1000 points of Guard as GSC really has a lot of internal synergies that need to work to make the army function and it’s hard to slot in Guard into that, but there are certainly pieces to use here.

Detachment Rule: Integrated Tactics

Continuing on to the second part of the rule, in the Shooting phase each time an Astra Miliatrum unit is selected to shoot it can select an enemy unit within 18” and visible to it. It can only target that unit with its attacks this phase but that enemy is ‘caught in overlapping fire’ until the end of the phase. While a unit is caught in overlapping fire, each time a Genestealer Cults model from your army targets that enemy unit with a ranged attack, add 1 to the hit roll. This is a lot of words to say if a Guard model shoots one thing within 18” then GSC gets +1 to hit in the shooting phase. Even then it’s a lackluster rule as GSC is already an army that needs a lot of stacking buffs through multiple activations to get a strong output and adding another layer for that is rough especially since it will only be active for ranged attacks. As well, the ranged units that can take advantage of this are exactly Neophyte Hybrids and Achilles Ridgerunners, which isn’t the deepest range of threats. Overall it’s another hoop to jump through, but it does exist so it’s something we can use.

Enhancements

I’m doing my best here to be positive about this Detachment, and while some of these rules have in fact gotten a bit better in the new edition it’s still a pile of oddities that I don’t know if I would go out of my way to take.

  • Fire-Point Commander (10pts): GSC Infantry model only. Each time you target the bearer’s unit with the Fire Overwatch Stratagem, while resolving that Stratagem, hits are scored on an unmodified hit roll of a 5+. This is pretty decent as it basically affords you a secondish shooting activation with your heavy weapons that normally hit on 5s anyways. That being said, while Neophytes with a Benefictus are the ideal target for this, I’m not super sold; I would usually prefer to overwatch with the bounty of flamers we can still field, so I think it is list dependent.
  • Adaptive Reprisal (15pts): GSC Infantry model only. When you target this unit with the Heroic Intervention Stratagem, that use is -1CP. This would be great if this Detachment did anything in melee. I can see it going on an Iconward Neophyte squad or maybe an Abominant with Aberrants, with either unit just there to help bog down attacks, but it is still something I’m not super excited for. That being said, it does allow you to do the 6” heroic on turn 1 if your opponent goes first, which can help deter some very aggressive turn 1 move blocks.
  • Martial Espionage (25pts): GSC Infantry model only. Once per turn when a friendly Astra Militarum Infantry or Mounted unit within 9” of the bearer is selected to shoot, the bearer can use this enhancement and give those ranged attacks +1 AP until the end of the phase. Actually pretty good, I won’t lie; especially with the cover changes in 11th edition no longer giving an AP buff, you actually can make a large volume of attacks functionally hurt a lot more this edition, which is nice. I’ve had this in a few lists I’ve run and a wounded Krieg squad that revives its meltas and plasmas to then shoot an enemy with +1 to hit, wound, and AP is a randomly scary threat that can catch people off guard.
  • The Hero Returned (20pts): GSC Infantry model only. Improve the Leadership and Objective Control characteristics of models in the bearer’s unit by 1. Actually a crazy good strat when paired with extra healing from the Xenocult Detachment and an Iconward for a 5+ Feel No Pain. Now you can bog down the center objective with a load of 3OC Neophytes that have a Feel No Pain and regenerate 6-9 models. I think this is a steal.

Stratagems

Two of these don’t currently work and one only works on a 3+ dice roll. I am not a fan but I must tell you about them against the better judgement of my soul.

  • A Dark Network (1CP): During the reinforcement step of your opponent's movement phase, just after an enemy unit is set up on the battlefield, one friendly GSC or Astra Militarum unit within 12”of that enemy unit can make a normal move of 6”. Well, the reinforcement step no longer exists, thusly this stratagem does not have a legal timing window. You can house rule it to ignore that, but RAW this doesn’t work. That being said, when it did work it was pretty decent in some matchups and irrelevant into others.
  • Symbiotic Destruction (1CP): One Astra Militarum and one GSC unit get re-roll 1s to wound but must shoot the same visible target that they are both within range of. This is actually really good and something I would say is worth using a lot to handle the tougher bricks of your opponent’s army. Giving the aforementioned Kriegers reroll 1s to wound while they might have their +1 to hit/wound active is good, and Neos have enough volume that this is going to be affecting a lot of dice. That being said, it does lock these units into only shooting the one unit, so there is no split firing and if one unit kills it by themselves then the other unit cannot shoot anything else that phase.
  • Acceptable Losses (2CP): In your shooting phase, one Astra Militarum unit in your army can shoot at an enemy unit that is within engagement range of a GSC unit from your army. After resolving those attacks, roll one d6 for each GSC unit that was in engagement range of that enemy unit: on a 5+, that GSC unit takes D3+1 mortal wounds. This is pretty costly at D3+1 mortals, but I think overall this is more than fine and can even help free up a unit that is being tagged up by just a few chaff models from an opponent’s army. So, situational but not something that is a waste of a Stratagem slot.
  • Regimental Reinforcements (1CP): During your opponent’s Shooting phase or the fight phase when an Astra Militarum Infantry Regiment unit is destroyed. Roll a d6: on a 3+ add a new unit to roster that is identical to the destroyed unit at Starting Strength and place it into Cult Ambush. You can only use this stratagem once per battle. I trimmed a bit of the fat explaining it but essentially when they kill one of your Guard units, spend a CP to roll a 2 to never be able to waste a CP on this stratagem for the game. That’s right, even if you fail the 3+ you cannot use this stratagem again later on to try and get back at least one unit during the game which is a really big let down. When it does work, however, it’s still pretty good and can really help with horde style lists that want to run as many bodies as possible as bringing back 20 Krieg with this is akin to bringing 20 Neos and that’s 6 whole Resurgence Points. I’m torn on this strat because I would like it honestly to just be 2CP and automatically go off but we are here. Use it if you’re playing swarm or want more Kasrkin for more mortals.
  • Suppress and Overwhelm (1CP): In your shooting phase just after an Astra Militarum unit has shot an enemy unit. Select one enemy unit hit by one or more of those attacks and until the end of the turn that enemy unit cannot be the target of the Fire Overwatch Stratagem and each time that unit is charged by a GSC unit, the GSC unit gets to re-roll the Charge roll. That’s a lot of words to say, “Your GSC units get to re-roll charges against something a Guard unit shot” because the first half of this stratagem doesn’t work anymore, although it didn’t really work in 10th either, but I digress. Yeah this is bad because you also have no benefits in the fight phase from this Detachment, so charging enemy units is just doing so with unsupported GSC melee units and I’m not the biggest fan of that.
  • In the Shadows of Iron (1CP): When an enemy unit ends a move within 8” of a cult ambush marker you can move that marker to be 8” away from enemy models and within 6” of an Astra Militarum Vehicle unit from your army. I almost always feel nothing when I think about the ambush marker stratagems from GSC Detachments. You don’t really need to do this but I guess it can be cute in the perfect scenarios.

After playing several games with this Detachment, I will let you know the most used stratagems were: Explosives, Rapid Ingress, and Go To Ground Heroic Intervention. I hope that illustrates just how impactful these six stratagems are. Small sidenote: It’s been three dataslates since the new edition dropped; how are there two entire stratagems that just do not work still? Is it genuinely acceptable to just not care so much about a faction that you can’t be bothered to update rules that try to function with incorrect timings or in phases that no longer exist? Can GW stop fumbling GSC and actually support the faction in a meaningful way instead of just giving us scraps and nerfing our points whenever someone finally does well with them? What would happen if Gladius went through three dataslates and a third of its rules still just didn’t work? I’ll end it there because I don’t want to come off as unprofessional but I genuinely care about this faction and even though Brood Brothers isn’t the sub-faction for me, the people who do enjoy it should have their time, money, and energy that they put into the hobby respected.

Playing This Detachment

Brood Brothers is a bit of a mess and its rules aren’t the cleanest, but this faction holds a very cherished spot in the hearts of a lot of GSC and Guard players, figuring into everything from fun creative builds that feature Aberrants running alongside a Baneblade at your local game store to the sweatiest of games where I’m dropping 250 bodies onto the table and making my opponent experience actual trench warfare. The Detachment doesn’t do enough, but the changes to 11th and the access it has to Detachments like Xenocult do give it a bit of a facelift and can actually solve its problem of zero damage. That being said, I think that what we have here needs a fundamental rewrite as the lists you make in this are most often just better off as either GSC or Astra Militarum and that doesn’t feel good.

Strengths

  • Diversity. Kind of scraping the bottom of the barrel here but the fact that this detachment gives you 2 army ranges to pull from does mean that the styles of lists you can make varies greatly and I’ve see a lot of different lists that are teched to handle different archetypes.
  • Objective Control. When I ran this list to a 5-0 finish it included 120 Death Korps of Krieg and 120 Neophyte Hybrids that flooded the board and stopped my opponents from ever holding the point. I think that you can still very much do that today, but it’s going to be a challenge for sure

Weaknesses

  • Rules. The Detachment brings you 1000 points of Guard and two broken stratagems to support your shooting side of GSC. There are no melee buffs here and you can’t even run Ogryn next to Aberrants to make a thick bruiser style list. 

A Sample List

I’m sure you will be shocked to discover that Brood Brothers Auxilia doesn’t have the biggest showing of results. I will say that there is still some room to be played with a variant I affectionately call “Brood Bolt,” where you focus on bringing units that focus on dealing Mortal Wounds through Melta Mines and Demolition Charges to whittle your opponents down to let the Xenocult side of your army finish them off. It’s a very fun list and if you do want to get into trying out Brood Brothers I’d say give it a try!

Final Thoughts

I’ll be very honest and open here, for a long time I have really talked down on this Detachment saying it wasn’t good and should be avoided. I think those statements were misguided and unproductive. When this Detachment works together it does feel really cool and it genuinely can be a lot of fun and that should be encouraged. One of the most deeply ingrained parts about the Astra Militarum and Genestealer Cults is their complicated history with one another and I think a Detachment that represents that coalition should have the actual support and respect for its rules like every other Detachment and army does. However, at time of writing I don’t think that is accomplished and it’s not the failure of the player for it being in this state. I'd urge the team that works on the next GSC Codex to really take time and understand how and why this version of the Detachment failed so that you can better learn from it and succeed next time. I want to sing your praises, so please give me something worth doing so.

title: Can the reskin of Warhammer 40k: Forbidden Stars improve on the original?
content:
How do you transplant a strategy game from the grim darkness of the far future into the psychedelic chaos at the dawn of the universe? That's the challenge for board game designer Samuel Bailey, whose new game Old Ones Origins takes his earlier design Warhammer 40,000 Forbidden Stars, and transports its galaxy conquering action out of the Imperium of Man and into the Cthulhu Mythos. I interviewed him to find out what was changing, and what elements of that classic design will stay the same.

Forbidden Stars was released in 2015, only a year before Fantasy Flight Games lost the license to make Warhammer 40,000 titles, giving it a very short but fondly remembered lifespan. Bailey co-designed it with James Kniffen, the duo adapting an earlier Starcraft Board Game that Corey Konieczka and Christian T. Petersen made for FFG in 2007.

All told, Call of Cthulhu: Old Ones Origins will be the third published iteration of the rules - and there have almost been other editions. "I've gone through three publishers with this, and I've done a different version for [each of] them - I had a whole version that I had made that was more hard sci-fi in a setting that I created myself", Bailey says. When he signed up with Chaosium, moving the game to the Cthulhu Mythos was obvious.

But it's not the Cthulhu Mythos as you might know it. "There's so much sci-fi where it's very human-centric - I want to do sci-fi that just has no humans in it, and can just be as imaginative and interesting as possible." So the new game is set in the very earliest days of reality, when the Lovecraftian Great Old Ones aren't ancient mysteries, they're emperors and warlords grappling for control of the universe.

I've already written a separate article delving into the character and playstyle of the four Great Old Ones that will come in the core game set currently up on crowdfunding platform Gamefound. Forbidden Stars did an excellent job giving the four Warhammer 40k factions it featured distinct mechanical identities - when Bailey reminisces about it, we get a glimpse at what might have been if Fantasy Flight had kept the Warhammer 40k license, and a promising hint at what might be in store for Old Ones Origins if the game sells well.

"I had a lot of ideas that I was excited to get to, like Necrons, and Tyranids, and Dark Eldar, and T'au", Bailey says. "My idea was to do another full box core set with new tiles, and you could mix and match everything, rather than just drip feed one faction at a time". Another idea was "to do mini expansions through the print on demand factory, using the same minis, but [for example] a deck of all the Space Wolves cards" - that was kaiboshed by the terms of the licensing agreement, which would have required Space Wolf models to go with Space Wolf cards.

Surprisingly, working with the Lovecraft mythos isn't without restrictions. "While all of Lovecraft's stuff is in the public domain, not everything in the Lovecraft mythos is, and there's quite a few prominent monsters that actually were not invented by Lovecraft and are still under the ownership of various authors". "Chaosium has a lot of agreements with that for the role-playing game", he adds, "but not with board game stuff".

The distinctive makeup of the Mythos has also posed a challenge for making full factions. "You need a god who's been written about a lot, to hang narrative and mechanical hooks on, and has a lot of units that you can put under their banner that makes sense", Bailey says. "It was very easy to do for Warhammer 40K because everything is already in the game, there's plenty of units and abilities to draw from", he continues, "but it's been surprisingly challenging to build out these factions". Lovecraft was big on big guys, but the middle rungs of faction hierarchy have taken a little creative license to fill out.

Much of the mechanical identity of Forbidden Stars came from the asymmetrical factions and the way their mechanics matched their lore - an approach which, when followed through to the Lovecraft Mythos, inevitably results in very different factions. "My goal was to make it make a game that still feels like Forbidden Stars, but change as much as possible", Bailey says.

And there have been more systematic changes. For one, units don't have a Morale stat to represent their bravery and sanity any more. "That didn't really make sense in a Cthulhu universe with the great Eldritch beings with alien minds", Bailey says. It's replaced by Power, a Call of Cthulhu RPG stat that reflects magical ability, and in Old Ones Origins fills a different mechanical role. Where Morale decided the victor in conflicts after three rounds of fighting, players can now exhaust their units to provide Power points, helping them to to cast spell cards from their hand.

The combat system has have received quite a lot of tinkering, informed by feedback on the original game. "One criticism of Forbidden Stars is the length of the conflicts", which only ever involve two players, "and sometimes you're just sitting there for 10, 15 minutes until several people have had conflicts that you're not involved in". Conflicts in Old Ones Origins can be multiplayer brawls, and in certain "nexus zones" it's possible for players to participate with their spells and conflict cards even if they have no units.

This is a design that Bailey has been developing in one form or another for over a decade now. One of the most enjoyable parts of the interview was how enthusiastic he still is for the game after all that time - he mentioned many more small tweaks that only veterans of the original title are likely to appreciat. I'm still hoping to arrange a virtual demo with him - the first place you'll get to hear my thoughts is in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture Review, Part 3 of 4 - White, Blue, and Black Cards
content:
At the crossroads of Jace’s rampant egomania and ‘what if I drew a fucked up, evil version of the Hamburger Helper’ lies Reality Fracture, Magic’s newest set. This is the first Planeswalkers-matter set since 2019’s War of the Spark, or should we say Planeswalker, singular, as Jace is the set’s focal point. Reality Fracture is filled with powerful cards and their alternate universe counterparts, offering both novel mechanical takes on beloved characters, and imaginative ‘what-if’ scenarios for Vorthoses. To that end, this set is built for pick-2 draft, with both versions of many characters appearing alongside one another in the same pack. After a couple of middling releases, this set is probably the most powerful since Avatar, and we expect a host of multi-format staples to solidify once players get their hands on Reality Fracture. Today we’re covering the set’s white, blue, and black cards.

Reality Fracture officially releases to tabletop on October 2nd, and on Magic: The Gathering Arena on September 29th.

White

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Ajani Resolute

Saffgor: 2 mana Planeswalkers are a rarity as it is, and good ones even moreso. I think this is more Wrenn than Tibalt, though, and seems like a great pickup for lifegain strategies.

BPhillipYork: This should be gaining loyalty counters pretty fast even in a commander game, maybe even fast enough to deal with random flyers and such hitting it.  It's a neat design and I'd like to see more planeswalkers be viable.

FromTheShire: Now that's one hell of a card. Your average lifegain deck generates what I would ballpark as 3 triggers per game action by any player so you can expect Ajani to be a constant thorn in the side if he's not dealt with. By the end of the game you're going to wish they were popping the ultimate rather than a never ending supply of ever growing beaters.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Campus Crier

Saffgor: This is lowkey one of the best Empower enablers, being something you can mill over and activate in the yard for cheap, which then provides a target for your Reality Scrambles or Entrust the Sparks. Popping this on the opponent's End Step and untapping with your Scramble effect is very real. It matters less in Commander, but in a 60 card version of the combo I think it has a key role. Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Danitha, Sword of Hope

BPhillipYork: Solid enabler for two kinds of decks, or both combined. Really useful for Equipment decks which don't have a ton of good card draw sources, and kind of neat to have protecting your creatures also have some card draw attached for replacement.

FromTheShire: She's not as good as Sram, but that's a high bar to clear, and you'll likely be happy to get the redundancy. Plus she has the upside of also drawing off of pump and protection spells so you may occasionally get a second draw per turn cycle, though it won't be a regular occurance.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Enlightened Confidant

Saffgor: The game is a bit too fast to make this wildly compelling, and that’s a sad thing. This should be good, I feel it in my bones, but it probably isn’t.

BPhillipYork: This is a really nice payoff for lifegain decks. Decent creature to have lifegain on top of that to set up it's own trigger, though a bit flimsy.

FromTheShire: It's definitely better in 60 card than Commander, but we do already have some lifegain decks there that will be very happy to see it. There's no world where it even comes close to eclipsing Bob since it is a build around rather than being generically powerful but I like it. Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Flickering Hound

Saffgor: The trigger isn’t my concern with this card, it’s the targets. Plenty of ways to spam out Creatures, but it’s much harder to make this go mana-neutral or mana-positive, by virtue of it not being able to target Artifacts (e.g. mana rocks). Still good, but it’s no kitten.

BPhillipYork: There's some obvious comparison to Displacer Kitten here but it's nowhere near as good. It really feels like she should though.

BPhillipYork: Good self-mill, presumably set up to reanimate something specific. For Commander that's a bit dicey given the 1 of format and large deck size, but if you've got a number of useful targets, or just want to fill your yard it's a low cost way to keep milling away. Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Loot, the Anomaly

Saffgor: This is the kind of little freak that Reality Fracture is all about. He’s not good, but you can definitely Agatha’s a Hyalopterous Lemure under him and swing out for game. It’s not about being good though, it’s about being weird, and in that domain Black Loot excels.

FromTheShire: This is an interesting commander to do lower tier Voltron with, especially since it gives you a reason to play with Hyalopterous Lemure and Viscid Lemures, noted cards I'm sure you're all familiar with. Stuff them in an Agatha's Soul Cauldron and now you're one shot K.O.-ing people. Dumb? Yes. Fun? Also yes.

BPhillipYork: Yay for weird rules conundrums. There's definitely lots of ways to pump down his power, and sort of a fun thing to build, if not amazingly good. Sort of strange that WotC have devolved to the point where they just have a card that's "the McGuffin". Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Mabel, Bitter Recluse

Saffgor: If this said permanent, we'd be talking, but as it stands Mabel's just not going to compare with something like Vampire Hexmage.

FromTheShire: I'm on the fence with this one, she's a rattlesnake that can also snipe planeswalkers for one mana, but without knowing how the meta is going to shake out it's hard to say if that will be worth much. Maybe she offers some upside as a ninjutsu piece.

BPhillipYork: There's a few fun things you could remove with this, things that uptick with negative counters, or use it in conjunction with blight. Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Multiply by Zero

Saffgor: I'll buck the trend and say this is mediocre, about comparable to a Go for the Throat. Most things that have Indestructible in Commander are Voltron-adjacent, and probably also have counters or Equipment/Auras.

FromTheShire: Solid removal spell with the upside of being able to deal with indestructible creatures, I like it.

BPhillipYork: Wow that's really strong creature control. Really just removes anything that is targetable, basically can't be protected. Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Overwrite the Multiverse

Saffgor: Another way to Empower Jace for 8+ for Kasmina, or push you forward for Reality Sculptor. Great card if you’re in the colors for it, and playing towards one of those endgames. Bad elsewhere.

FromTheShire: A mass exile sweeper in black is awesome to get access to. Oh, and I guess it also makes a big Jace token after, sure.

BPhillipYork: Well that's quite a strong board clear, though expensive. I feel like overwriting the universe should really require all 5 colors, and to have it be pure black is just kind of lazy. Like WotC doesn't understand the implications of their own IP, but given the profusion of nonsensical and lazy Universes Beyond, then obviously they don't, or they just don't really care. Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Rise of the Deathbringer

Saffgor: 5 mana Instant-speed -3/-3 is a ruthless profile for control, even disregarding the draw mode. Being able to hold up mana for a not-insignificant board wipe like that will dunk midrange, and maybe even aggro if you’re on a little ramp. The draw mode is worse than the original Return of the Wildspeaker, but I think this card on the whole is better.

FromTheShire: Massive amounts of card draw or a mini board wipe at instant speed, what's not to like?

BPhillipYork: This is a fractured version of Return of the Wildspeaker and it's probably stronger, though regular return is a solid finisher, this is a nice modal spell too. -3/-3 is generally going to clear almost everything off the board, or you can just card draw. Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Sanctum Lurker

Saffgor: I’m shocked this isn’t Legendary, because it feels like the kind of wacky text they’d aim to place on a Commander. That being said, as a card this requires your opponents play Creature removal and not simply bowl over your Planeswalkers with damage, and that’s reasonable insulation for something like a Gideon of the Trials. You could probably get some mileage out of creating a ‘Secret Commander’ deck with this at the helm, though the actual Commander would need to put in some work, like Aminatou.

FromTheShire: Horror is right. If you can actually stick this and protect it you immediately turn off the whole issue with planeswalkers in Commander, namely that they usually are cast, activate once, and then die. Notably loyalty can't go negative, so no matter how hard they get hit your walkers will happily keep sitting at 0, ready to use either the plus granted here or their built in ones to start ticking right back up into problematic territory.

BPhillipYork: Yeah I don't like this really, it just overwrites the rules of the game and it has potential to just let you keep stax planeswalkers sitting around. Some of the best early ones cost only 3 like Ashiok, Dream Render, and if they just won't die then that's really rough. Thankfully it's a creature so relatively easy to remove. Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Teyo, Diamondblade Mage

Saffgor: Giving weird Enchantments Deathtouch can result in repeatable, Instant-speed boardwipes. That’s extremely cool, as is the capacity to turbo out Black Planeswalkers’ ultimates, which tend to win the game on resolution. The issue stems from the fact that Black Teyo is 4 mana, unlike his 2-mana White counterpart, which is a shame. Were this cheaper, I’d honestly be writing a Commander Focus on the guy, because this effect genuinely is novel. Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Tinybones, Pocket Nuisance

Saffgor: This is just worse than other Tinybones-es, though in Standard it could perhaps be a piece for discard?

FromTheShire: If you build around him Tinybones is going to be more than a pocket sized nuisance. Even when he drops he's making 3 people discard a card and dealing 3 damage, and then his discard is not keyed to only when opponents discard, so if you want to you can teach your opponents all about cleanup step looping strategies as you ping them to death.

BPhillipYork: Wow. Really solid 3-drop, pinging people for discarding and doing it when he enters. All the Tinybones in conjunction are starting to get really mean and have a lot of synergy. Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Vraska's Final Mercy

Saffgor: {B}{B} cost and Empower 6 are both really unfortunate breakpoints, which likely precludes this card from being played in the Islands-matter Jace shell. Good in Limited, at least.

FromTheShire: Sorcery speed is a bummer, but the rate on killing a planeswalker or making a big Jace token is quite good.

BPhillipYork: Good creature control for 2 mana, and there's modal empowerment of Jace if you want that. Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Way of the Necromancer

Saffgor: My pick for the best Way Enchantment, Way of the Necromancer is absolutely wild. Tons of Black Planeswalkers make chaff bodies you can throw under an Altar, and Bx decks in general have an aristocrats bent. This is cheap, at bare minimum likely cantrips, and can help you push for endgames with deathloops or ultimates way ahead of schedule. It’s shocking they’re printing this card, and it goes to show the expected power of Planeswalkers in modern Magic is defined by Commander, and not 60-card. In the format that is aggressively hostile to the card type, the designers are doing their damndest to make them playable. Is this really what it takes?

FromTheShire: Good Christmas that's a lot of counters. Even if you only have a few walkers out using their abilities to create creature tokens which you can then use to block to protect your squad and refill their loyalty it means it's going to be an uphill climb to deal with your board. However, we're in black, aka the color of sacrificing and reanimation loops, and so in reality this is going to read as 'Ultimate each planeswalker you control', and that tends to win games.

BPhillipYork: This is one of the ways to easily ult off by sacrificing a bunch of creatures for value to ult out something you just dropped, like a Liliana Vess, in which case everything just pops back into play.

Next Time: The Set’s Red and Green Cards

That wraps up our look at the White, Blue, and Black cards of Reality Fracture. We’ll be back next week to wrap our review up with the Red and Green cards.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@goonhammer.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and more.

title: Mayday, Miss Marcy! True Horror Stories
content:
Welcome back dear readers once again to Mayday, Miss Marcy, our regular advice column in which your reader submitted questions are answered by me, with a dose of honesty and potential comedy (YMMV). This week our column falls exactly on the first of the month, and for October 1st, that means two things: It was my birthday yesterday, and we're now within the 31 day window in which Halloween and all things spooky and horrific are allowed before Christmas takes over the remaining 60 days of the year (At least in the United States).

Perhaps just in time to kick off October, I have 3 pretty horrific questions for this week. AS a note, I did reach out to all 3 of these askers to ensure they were okay with the questions and answers, and they respond positively! Why? Well, you might see, if you dare... (But as a non-joke, a few of these have some minor content warnings).

If you're curious to have your own (hopefully non-horrific) questions answered here, then please follow the instructions below:

Have a question you want answered on just about anything you’d need advice on in this grand hobby space of ours? Board games, 40k, AOS, TTRPGs, MTG, anything and everything that we cover, we can help with!

For some examples, take a look at previous editions of our column at this link with a handy tag to see all previous questions and answers!

If you want to submit questions, we have a few ways you can do it. Patrons can use the Discord bot command to ask questions, which will be received anonymously!

If you’re not a Patron, or just don’t want extra steps, you can comment on this article, or e-mail me directly at marcy@tabletopbattles.com!

And here was last week's pretty positive set of questions, perhaps as a good palette cleanser.

Parasocial Paralysis

Miss Marcy,

I'm writing to you on behalf of my gaming group, or, we are writing to you, but I'm the one who is sending you the message because I'm the patron and can use Gregbot. My gaming group has a... problem. I hesitate to call him a stalker, and we debated calling him a leech, but that feels dehumanizing. The problem is that when we go to our LGS to slam hams, there is a guy who will, almost like clockwork, show up and hang around our table. He doesn't play 40k, he doesn't know any of us beyond having figured out our names through osmosis, and we don't know or have ever interacted with him.

Now before anyone asks, yes the store is open to the public, so this guy is obviously welcome to be in the store and we don't have any way to control that ourselves. He also isn't... aggressive, or weird, or anything, but he really has begun bringing the mood of our group down because he has kind of attached himself to our group and acts like we are friends; I couldn't even say I know his name! We've talked to the owner of the LGS who has basically said that since he's not doing anything wrong, he has no reason to ban him, which felt kind of like a non-answer. What do we do?

Group Paranoia

Dear Group,

So, this question has some uncomfortable aspects that we need to probably address first. One, the owner of this LGS sucks, because it is their job to establish a safe and welcoming environment, and it sounds like he is brushing off your group's concerns. Frankly, even if the guy is not being "weird", he is being weird. Just because he's not doing something aggressive or concerning, his behavior as you describe it is obviously making you all uncomfortable; we don't need to invent hypotheticals, the main thing here is you asked the owner of a LGS to help with another patron (who apparently doesn't even play the game, so does he even spend money there?) and they said not my problem.

I would probably start looking for a new LGS, if I were you, but let's also address your, well, leech. Did you ever watch What We Do in the Shadows with Colin the "Energy Vampire"? Essentially, a vampire that feeds off of other people's "energy" by being exhausting and socially unbearable. Your group has attracted an energy vampire, for lack of any better way to refer to him. He shows up when you all are playing, hangs around, apparently tries to use and know your names, and just... exists. The fact that none of you have told him to kindly go the hell away shows either an immense level of patience or perhaps some form of social cowardice in that you feel bad for him, which is not helping either party.

You are a group of adults, I assume, and if this random other adult is making you uncomfortable, ask him to go away. If the LGS owner has abdicated helping you, you will need to probably just go "hey man, we don't really know you, can you go the hell away"? But, let's be potentially charitable. Have you all ever asked this guy if he wants to play? Because although I do think the behavior is a little weird and uncomfortable, my charitable side of reading this is that perhaps he is a shy and socially awkward person who wants to play but is afraid to ask, and just seems to hope that by being around, it will happen through osmosis. I think you could even ask if he wants to play, or learn to play, and if you find that isn't palatable or remains weird, you should tell him to buzz off, raise the problem with the LGS owner, and then I think start looking for somewhere to play.

A True Horror Story

CW: This question deals with tampered with food and drugging / spiking a drink.
Marcy,

I don't have an easy way to start this question. I was drugged at a gaming event held at my LGS, which only came to light because I was not the only person it happened to. My LGS had tried a 21+ gaming night, which allowed alcohol to be brought. I do not need the lecture about open containers, all I will say is anyone who thinks it can't happen quickly should know that what happened to me was, at my best guess, done in a few seconds in which my attention had been taken away. The brazen act is probably why they were caught, because they apparently didn't know which drink was actually mine, and also spiked another drink. "Thankfully" my friend was affected before I was, and we both cannot remember the night after a certain point, but others at the event called 911 when we apparently both started acting strange and one of us fell over. The person was caught, and that part is handled.

My question, really, is... what do I even do? How do I actually just go back to going to events? I wanted to play games because I am not really the type to go clubbing, I don't find bars and other places enticing or comfortable, and all the usual reasons one might have anxiety over this sort of thing happened... at my lgs. I can't even really stomach going back, despite a lot of promises for help, support, and even how the group/store acted, I just don't know how to go back. I realize this is a HEAVY question but... what do I do?

Struggling

Dear Struggling,

First, as a note to our readers, I did get in touch with Struggling before answering this question and provided some suggestions in those conversations, but I also asked if they wanted me to really publish this question, which they said they would like to in order to try and move on. 

My summary answer is:

Dear Struggling, I cannot even begin to imagine how horrific that is, and just the absolute violation of safety of yourself and others for what can only be assumed were far worse implications that did not come to be. That this person was so craven to recklessly attempt this and endangered multiple people is honestly vile, and I can't probably publish what I hope happens to them. 

I think I... do not actually know the answer to your question. 

On the one hand, I want to say that you should cut your loss and protect yourself, perhaps looking for a new place or a new shop and group. But the group is also who stepped in immediately to protect you and the other person, despite this other person's actions. I realize that the location can seem ruined, but the people at your store seem to be good people who did the right thing. I hesitate to try and prescribe an action because I think most people would struggle here, and I don't blame them! I do say that I would maybe talk to any friends you have who still go, or even the owner; it sounds like the store itself made a choice that was ruined and preyed on by a predator, but the store itself is not the problem. I urge you not to give up on your hobbies, though, even if it means moving on from this location, and I'm so sorry you had to go through any of this. 

Survivor's Guilt

CW: This question references suicide and death.
Dear Miss Marcy,

Back in February, my local gaming group was shocked by the sudden suicide of one of our regular members. This person was always friendly, polite, approachable, a pleasure to play against and with, all sorts of things. This probably sounds really stereotypical. As you might expect, no one could say anything but good things but then they were gone and our community has never really recovered. We've had a lot of members leave, lots of bouts of fighting and other things, and the only reason I've written you is that I actually ended up moving, and have just wanted to get a few thoughts out.

I don't really know what we, or me, were supposed to do. When it happened, the usual went around: people were sorry to hear, horrified, oh they were so nice, all of it. But none of us really knew this person, apparently. We didn't know what was going on, nor could we do anything about it. All sorts of pretty vile things were said to others in FB comments, people destroyed friendships, and it just all felt awful. Everything after the fact was handled so badly that most of us had no idea how to support anyone, if there was a funeral, anything.

I guess the thing I'm struggling with now is that, in my new home, I'm relucant to join a community again. I'm 34, I have a job and personal social circle, and I'm not exactly struggling for interaction. But when I think about joining a gaming group, I'm left thinking about what if it happens again? Do I just not make friends? Do I bother?

Surviving

Dear Surviving,

Your question is, tragically, relatable. The older I get, the more people I lose, and for many different reasons. Before this sounds like I am making it about myself, I want to simply say that unfortunately death becomes more familiar to people than others, and that as you get older, you start to get more acquainted with them.

It does not get easier.

Whatever the reasons for this person's choice, I hate that the scenario you described is also very... relatable. Death is huge, and it leaves a hole that a lot of people do not know how to manage. Some people prefer to simply fill it in, pretend the hole didn't exist, while others want to preserve the respect the hole; there's all sorts of healthy and unhealthy ways death is dealt with. For you, I suppose, it was managed by moving away, but it also sounds like that community was spiraling out due to what happened.

As to your actual question of what to do... I think you should do whatever makes you happy and comfortable. I think you are maybe asking me, a neutral, anonymous party, something you've already decided, which is "can I just give up this hobby". I think the answer is yes. You can give it up, because it is a hobby. But the problem is that your hobby isn't the actual issue, it is people's interactions and social networks. Any group you join after this can always have this problem arise; people die. It is a fact of life. Should that prevent you from making new friends? No. You shouldn't cut yourself off of things you like, of making new connections, solely to protect yourself from seeing the uglier side of what can happen when the inevitable occurs.

I urge you to find ways to interact with others; if giving up gaming and doing something else is how you can move on, do it, but don't give up on socializing solely for that reason. The games don't matter; the people do, and you're one of them. Isolating yourself and not engaging with things you like isn't going to help anyone, especially yourself. I hope you find some new people and places to do things you enjoy, and that you can move on.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Critical Role's Luis Carazo tells us why you should play more than just D&D
content:
"For me, the system really does frame how you're going to experience the story." In a recent Wargamer interview, Critical Role campaign 4 star Luis Carazo told me a little about his process as an actual play actor. There's a tremendously deep creative and psychological background that goes into creating a character like Azune Nayar, but one key tenet? It's playing more games than just Dungeons and Dragons.

Carazo is no stranger to other systems, and his actual play credits pay testament to that. Before campaign four, he was best known for his roles in Candela Obscura, Vampire: The Masquerade's L.A. By Night, Outbreak: Undead's Rag & Bone, and Werewolf: The Apocalypse's Vancouver By Night. He's explored many more games through one-shots, too - just recently, Carazo took part in a Gen Con demo of 13 Omens, a new horror system from Pathfinder publisher Paizo.

Carazo says playing a variety of RPGs "helps me crack open the box that tends to form when I'm playing one particular system for a long time." For him, "there's certain systems that cause you to lean into different themes and different dangers". He tells me social-driven systems like World of Darkness are "part of the reason I might be a pretty good Schemer". Similarly, Outbreak: Undead presents "a survival horror system where the odds are stacked against you".

These games, unlike D&D, have slightly higher stakes when it comes to things like death. "The mechanics of the system determine how dangerous the world is to a great extent", Carazo explains. "In Dungeons and Dragons, death is not that dangerous when you have so many ways to avoid it or come back from it."

Death is a little more dangerous in Aramán thanks to some homebrew choices from DM Brennan Lee Mulligan. However, Carazo says his diverse roleplaying experience helps him stay in a mindset that appreciates the stakes.

"Another system is definitely going to make you feel that the world is dangerous, because it makes you make harder choices more often. Playing in a survival horror setting changes your relationship to [your character's] moral compass."

All this helps build a character as richly conflicted as Azune. I ask Carazo what attracts him to this type of character.

"I was interested in someone in this sort of between state - culturally, identity-wise, self-esteem-wise - all these things in a grey area." "I think that has something to do with my psychology background", he adds. "I'm really interested in struggle and in people trying to make the most out of an impossible situation."

"I think of the character in those situations in terms of the pressure put upon them - how that's revealed, how we negotiate it, and how we might come to terms with parts of ourselves that are revealed and we may not like." "I like digging into 'who is the world forcing me to be? And who has the world denied me from being able to be?'"

Carazo also considers how the character exists within a specific setting. "How does this person, given what they've experienced, think the world sees them? What are the events and people that matter to them? How does he think those people see him?"

For Azune, the core realizations came quickly. "I have to be useful. I will never not be useful. That's a core part of his identity", Carazo explains. "The moment that was organically manifested in the game, it was like 'of course this is who he is'." "I have to remain useful, because something that becomes useless gets discarded."

"He's got a specific kind of arrested development", Carazo continues. "He's trapped in a sort of limbo of childhood adolescence, but there's a very adult side to him as well." "Early on, he would puff up his chest when he saw Kattigan and Teor for the first time to declare how grown up he was - which was in contrast with how grown up he actually is."

Regardless of system, roleplay proves fertile ground for exploring such a complex character. "You're discovering it as you go in its purest form", Carazo tells me. "That makes it fundamentally different from approaching a prepared, scripted role."

"You're still meant to embrace unpredictability within those parameters as well, but the frame is different when you don't even know what scenes are going to come up." "It's part of what makes it exhilarating and messy. I love it."

Luis had many more table stories to tell me, so I'll share the full interview on Wargamer's YouTube channel very soon! Until then, want to chat more about Critical Role? Join likeminded nerds in the Wargamer Discord. Or, if you want to do some roleplay of your own, check out our quick guide to the DnD classes.

Thoughts

Two unique builds face off in the final, which is just what we want to see! In the black and red corner, we've got an extremely toolboxy Martyrs Sisters build, which seems practically designed to delight me with how many options it has. In the green corner, Orks, sporting Zzap Gunwagons in place of some of the standard shooting pieces, creating a very crunchy target profile for foes to figure out, and also plenty of reach. The matchup is Priority vs. Purge, so the Sisters are trying to force through a count to 45 by Actioning centrally, while Purge needs to try and (deff)roll them off the table. Who wins?

In the Sisters favour, they're Martyrs so they can revive Characters, which gives them plenty of depth, and are set up to massively punish the Orks if they overextend (as the Triumph and Vahl between them provide incredible counterattack potential), so stops them from being aggressive they might like. They also have quite dense units, so picking stuff off for Kill More is non-trivial for the Orks. That cuts both ways though - it also means the Orks don't have to kill that many units before it starts really hurting for the Sisters in terms of keeping Actions or board presence going. Who comes off better?

Realistically, both these lists can win the game. I love Zzap guns in general, but they and Tankbustas don't have a massive number of ideal targets here, so the Sisters can prioritise other targets. On the other hand, the Orks are definitely going to kill some stuff, and every unit the Sisters lose sets them back.

As always when such things are streamed, I had a quick skim through the video, and the game does indeed look to have been very close. The game was on the Dawn of War layout for this mission, and Jean-Loup made the smart decision to deploy very turtled up in one corner. This forced the Orks to come and get him, and staggered when they arrived, and while they did so with gusto, they couldn't fully sweep the Sisters at speed. From there, it looks like Vahl refused to die on a really pivotal turn, giving the Sisters the momentum to take the game from that point. Well done to both players for making it into the finals in such a spectacular event, and congratulations to Jean-Loup.

Regardless - to focus on the positives, I very much agree with tripling up on Banshees in the current environment, especially as their ability to kill tougher Marines is completely unchanged. Double big Hawks is also very strong, and bringing a War Walker alongside them feels mandatory now. Even the Avatar, who I've been a little cold on recently, is another unit that soars in value without Oaths to worry about. This build even has two super obvious ways to spend the 15pts it gets in the update (either upgrade one Ranger unit to Scorpions, or buy the Autarch Aspect of Murder), and it's well set up to at least try Recon. Colin's already thriving here, and here's plenty of upside going forward, congratulations!
